paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 5.12 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 5)
paragraphs.text: (1) In addition to any other order or sanction that may be imposed, the Court may impose a penalty of 2 times the amount set out in item 3(1) of the tariff in Division 2 of Schedule C, or any larger or smaller amount the Court may determine, on a party who, without sufficient cause, (a) does not serve an affidavit of records in accordance with rule 5.5 or within any modified period agreed on by the parties or set by the Court, (b) does not comply with rule 5.10, or (c) does not comply with an order under rule 5.11. (2) If there is more than one party adverse in interest to the party ordered to pay the penalty, the penalty must be paid to the parties in the proportions determined by the Court. (3) A penalty imposed under this rule applies irrespective of the final outcome of the action.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.12:1 Rule 5.12 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.12. 1. Overview In H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., 2024 ABKB 424, Justice Marion sanctions under Rule 5.12: [115] A reasonable interpretation of rule 5.12 suggests that its purpose is to provide a monetary penalty, paid to the adverse party or parties, for failing to meet the time deadlines under rule 5.5, rule 5.10, or an order under rule 5.11. It is arguable that rule 5.12 could also apply to an on-time but deficient breach of discovery obligations. However, ensuring on-time delivery was the basis for the recommended rule: ALRI Consultation Memorandum 12.2 at xix, 12-14. [116] Although never expressly stated to be applicable to missed deadlines (rather than deficient disclosure), that interpretation is also consistent with the practice and comments of this Court in respect of rule 5.12: Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada v Tom 2003-1 Limited Partnership #2, 2010 ABQB 815 at para 26; Malton v Attia, 2015 ABQB 430 at para 117; Dornan (Re), 2016 ABQB 259 at para 15; McDonald & Bychkowski Ltd (CMB Insurance Brokers) v Lougheed, 2015 ABQB 792 at para 36; Peters v Keef, 2019 ABQB 398 at para 31; Minshull v LED Sign Supply Inc, 2019 ABQB 424 (Master) at paras 53-57; Song v Alberta, 2019 ABQB 789 (Master) at para 6; Clearbakk Energy Services Inc v Sunshine Oilsands Ltd, 2022 ABQB 506 at paras 12, 23. This was also the thrust of rule 5.12’s predecessor, former rule 190 of the former Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/1968 [Former Rules]; Johnston v Bryant, 2003 ABCA 169 at para 15. [117] I agree that the focus of rule 5.12 is on whether a party has met the deadline, however, I would not foreclose the possibility that a deficient affidavit of records, disclosure or compliance with a rule 5.10 order might also warrant a penalty under rule 5.12 where the timeline was facially met but the substance of requirement was not. This may be relevant where the Court is of the view that a penalty should be paid to the adverse party or parties, rather than the Clerk of the Court as is contemplated by rule 10.49. [118] Where rule 5.12 non-compliance is engaged in other aspects of an application, it may also be adequately addressed through a costs award rather than a penalty. [119] “Sufficient cause” under rule 5.12 is a “hard test” with a “high bar”, requiring “rare” and “extraordinary circumstances over which [a party] had no practical control”: Sun Life Assurance at para 26; Wagner v Petryga Estate, 2001 ABQB 690 at para 17. A party cannot complain where they are the architect of the delay or complications: Paraniuk v Pierce, 2018 ABQB 1015 at para 130. On the other hand, courts should be wary about encouraging wasteful proceedings that become more about imposing penalties than focussing on the merits of the action: Archer v Ribbon Communications Canada ULC, 2019 ABQB 481 at para 21. Where a penalty is warranted, it should be “readily identifiable on their facts”: Archer at para 21. Ultimately, even where there is not sufficient cause for non-compliance, the Court retains permissive discretion to decide whether to levy a rule 5.12 sanction: Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd v Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP, 2017 ABQB 626 at para 36, aff’d 2019 ABCA 2; Paraniuk at para 130. 2. Extending the Deadline for Filing In Chevalier v. Sunshine Village Corp., 2011 ABQB 295, 2011 CarswellAlta 700, 516 A.R. 1 (Master), the defendants applied for an order extending the time within which they would be required to file their affidavits of records. The individual defendant was in the process of bringing an application to strike out the claim as it related to him. In considering the issue, Master Laycock said, at paragraphs 10-14: 10 …. I note that both the existing and former rule, dealing with penalties for failing to file and serve an affidavit of records in time, imposes upon the party in default a requirement to show sufficient cause in order to avoid a penalty. The cases under the former rule state that the purpose of the rule was to ensure that litigation proceeds in an expeditious manner. 11 The new Foundational Rules emphasize that the purpose of the rules is to have claims fairly and justly resolved in a timely and cost-effective way. To achieve this the rules are intended to identify the real issues in dispute, facilitate a quick resolution at the least expense, and provide an effective, efficient and credible system of remedies and sanctions to enforce the rules. As earlier noted the purpose of Part 5 is to, among other things, encourage early disclosure. Rule 5.5(1) and (3) achieve this goal by fixing the time in which the defendants must file their affidavit. 12 The individual defendant emphasizes that if he is successful in striking out the claim, there would be no issues in dispute between the parties and to require him to file an affidavit of records would increase the cost of litigation. He argues that there is evidence from the pleadings and motions on the file and no further evidence is necessary to show that he has sufficient cause to extend his April 21, 2011 deadline for filing his affidavit of records. Pending the release of this decision I extended time for filing the Defendants affidavit of records. 13 To require the individual defendant to file an affidavit of records would be a wasted, expensive process if the statement of claim is struck in relation to him. At this stage of the proceeding it is not helpful to inquire at length into the grounds that the defendant is using in his motion to strike the statement of claim. It is sufficient that it does not appear to be frivolous or filed merely for the purpose of delay. I am satisfied that the efficiencies of time and expense would dictate that in this circumstance, there is sufficient cause to extend the time for the individual defendant to file his affidavit of records. Accordingly, the individual defendant will not be required to file his affidavit of records until 30 days after the hearing of his motion to strike the plaintiffs claim. 14 Arguably the circumstances are different for the corporate defendant. Its motion will not result in the plaintiffs' action being struck or dismissed. The best result would be to have the action severed on the basis that each plaintiff has a distinctive breach of contract action which should not be tried together. At least one of these plaintiffs will be allowed to continue his claim in this proceeding. Three of the four plaintiffs may be required to commence separate and individual actions, but this claim will, in some form, continue against the corporate defendant. 3. Rule Contrasted to Old Rule 190 In Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd. v. Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP, 2017 ABQB 626, 2017 CarswellAlta 1870, Justice C. Jones noted that the new Rule is less rigid. His Lordship said: 36 Rule 5.12, rather than rule 190, is now the applicable rule (see the transitional provisions in Part 15). The new rule is less punitive than the former rule. It reflects a shift away from the mandatory language of double costs to a more permissive, discretionary determination with respect to costs. Failure to comply no longer triggers strict liability, although the new rule does require a party to explain the circumstances to avoid sanction. 4. Meaning of “Without Sufficient Cause” I assume that the phrase “without sufficient cause” in the rule means that a Court has the discretion in appropriate circumstances, to excuse a party from the harsh imposition of the rule. Govenlock v. Govenlock (2001), 284 A.R. 396 (Master) at 398, per Master Breitkreuz. In the appeal from the decision, [see (2001), 284 A.R. 399 (Q.B.)], Lee J., at p. 401, agreed that such a discretion exists. In Wagner v. Petryga Estate, 2001 ABQB 690, 2001 CarswellAlta 991, 292 A.R. 320, Watson J. discussed what constitutes “without sufficient cause”. At pp. 324-325, His Lordship said: The concept of “without sufficient cause” is not a foreign one to legal discourse. In this context, it would seem to contemplate a form of reasonable excuse which is either beyond the control of the party upon whom the obligation falls or arises from the very complexity and difficulty necessarily associated with the requirement as applied to the particular case. The “cause” must be case specific, not generic. The terms of rule 188.1 shed some light on that interpretation since extensions can be granted due to the complexity of the case, or the volume or location of the records or other sufficient reason. I draw from the decision in Grzybowski[Grzybowski (Jaroslaw) et al. v. Fleming (Alexander) et al. (April 2, 2001), No. 9803 22727 (Alta. Q.B.), unreported; Quinn, MC.] that it was not incumbent upon the respondent to show that the respondent had been prejudiced by the delay in filing and service of the Affidavit of Records. More particularly, the fact that the respondent may have known that the appellant routinely wintered in Arizona is neither here nor there. The appellant could not impose a waiver of the rule upon the appellant by reason of such “notice”. To do so would also be a step back towards a requirement of a demand for the Affidavit of Documents. Moreover, a key object of the rule appears to be the larger benefit to the administration of civil justice by using sharp discipline to ensure that parties do not drag their feet. The terminology of the rule suggests that the court does not want to encourage parties to think waiver of that larger public interest can be assumed. In Balogun v. Pandher, 2003 ABQB 943, 2003 CarswellAlta 1620, 349 A.R. 390, 29 Alta. L.R. (4th) 195, Veit J. quoted Watson J.'s comment about “sufficient cause” with apparent approval (at p. 394). In Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Tom 2003-1 Ltd. Partnership No. 2, 2010 ABQB 815, 2010 CarswellAlta 2783, 516 A.R. 95, Justice Tilleman said, at paragraph 24–26: 24 In argument all parties agreed that the appropriate rule is Rule 5.12 of the new Alberta Rules of Court. All parties further agree the Respondents had missed a filing date by one week. 25 The new rule states: [text of Rule omitted] Both sides disputed what was intended by the language of “sufficient cause”(common to both old and new rules) and the differences between the more mandatory language of the original rule, (Rule 190) versus the discretionary language of the new Rule 5.12. Under the old Rule, Watson, J. (as he then was) explained the double costs penalty for late filing was intended to have a deterrent effect for parties who drag their feet. See Wagner v. Petryga Estate, 2001 ABQB 690, 292 A.R. 320; see also Johnston v. Bryant, 2003 ABCA 169, 327 A.R. 378 at para. 16. 26 Like its predecessor, Rule 5.12 uses “without sufficient cause” which I will explain below but I do not think a late party will find comfort under the new Rules just because the new 5.12 is now discretionary. I say this because the purposes of the new Rules include quickness in the resolution of a claim, timely communication, and efficiency including appropriate remedies and sanctions to enforce the rules. More specifically under the new Rule's section on Disclosure of Information, the purpose inter alia is to “… discourage conduct that unnecessarily or improperly delays proceedings …” Sufficient cause has been judicially addressed under the old Rule 190 and to me it still means a neglect that is excusable on sufficient grounds based on diligence of the party that has not been relieved by any other section of the Rules, or a statute, or a related Court ruling that may otherwise affect the disposition of the matter. On the last point see e.g. Anderson v. Airsprint Aircraft Management Inc., 2004 ABQB 12, 352 A.R. 59 at para. 31. Diligence means the filing party did everything it could but ran into extraordinary circumstances over which it had no practical control. Sufficient cause under Rule 5.12 will be a hard test to meet and certainly will never be captured by facts that suggest “oops, I forgot”. It is a Rule that contemplates excusable neglect but it faces a high bar. While excuses are rare, they may include such things as flood damage, fire, documented proof of failed courier, or sudden medical emergency. I only set out potential excuses to describe the extraordinary nature of the event, and not to describe a closed list. [Footnotes omitted] 5. Who Must Prove the Exemption? In Wagner v. Petryga Estate, 2001 ABQB 690, 2001 CarswellAlta 991, 292 A.R. 320, Watson J. held that the party seeking the exemption bears the onus of proving the appropriateness of an exemption. At p. 324, he said: The rule … imposes on the party claiming the exemption the proof of the exemption.

sentences.text: Obtaining records from others

paragraphs.text: (1) On application, and after notice of the application is served on the person affected by it, the Court may order a person who is not a party to produce a record at a specified date, time and place if (a) the record is under the control of that person, (b) there is reason to believe that the record is relevant and material, and (c) the person who has control of the record might be required to produce it at trial. (2) The person requesting the record must pay the person producing the record an amount determined by the Court.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.13:1 Rule 5.13 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.13. 1. Application of Rule Rule 209 should not be used to permit discovery of a person not a party if it amounts to a fishing expedition. The rule purports to deal with documents in the possession of a third person not a party to the action but does not relate to documents which are merely within the power and control of that person. Wachowich, J., in Miller (Ed) Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. et al. (1988), 63 Alta. L.R. (2d) 189, held at page 191: The British Columbia Court of Appeal in Rhoades v. Occidental Life Insurance Company of California… set out the standard of ‘probable relevance’ as the basis test for determining whether to order production of documents in the hands of a person not a party to the action … The court attached four caveats to the ‘probable relevance’ test: (1) the rule should not be used as a fishing expedition to discover whether or not a person is in possession of a document. (2) the documents need not necessarily be admissible in evidence at trial. (3) The documents of which production is sought must be adequately described, but not necessarily so specifically that they can be picked out from any number of other documents. (4) the parties' objections to production must be considered, but are not determinative. I accept this approach, with the additional condition that the rule cannot be used as a method of obtaining discovery of a person not a party to the action. As Mr. Justice Thompson of the Ontario High Court said in Markowitz v. Toronto Transit Comm., [1965] 2 O.R. 215 at 217, when considering the Ontario equivalent of R. 209(1): Rule 349 was never intended to be used merely as a means of obtaining discovery from a stranger to the action, nor for exploratory purposes alone …Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1989), 98 A.R. 374 at 382 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1990), 74 Alta. L.R. (2d) 262 (C.A.)]. In the Court of Appeal Esso decision, Stevenson J.A. said at pp. 265-66 [74 Alta. L.R. (2d)]: In my view this rule should not be used against a non-party unless it can be shown that the document is in existence and not available through other means; in this case, through a party. If the document is relevant, and was in the possession of the plaintiffs, they are required to disclose its existence under R. 186, and may be asked about its disposition in the course of oral discovery. I also agree with the Chief Justice that this form of production should be related to specific documents of at least probable relevance and is not a form of discovery of a non-party. The Supreme Court of Canada in Frenette v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., [1992] 1 S.C.R. 647, had occasion to comment upon the equivalent British Columbia rule. The court spoke with approval of the B.C. C.A.'s interpretation of the British Columbia rule. It is fair to conclude that the court's comments are applicable to the Alberta rule. At pp. 691-92 the Supreme Court of Canada said: Similarily, in British Columbia, rule 26(11) of the Supreme Court Rules provides: Where a document is in the possession or control of a person who is not a party, the court, on notice to the person and all other parties, may order production and inspection of the document or preparation of a certified copy that may be used instead of the original. The manner in which a court should exercise its discretion under rule 26(11) as well as the scope of information which may be communicated to an applicant was spoken to by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Dufault v. Stevens (1978), 6 B.C.L.R. 199. The British Columbia Court of Appeal took an approach analogous to the one chosen in Cook[Cook v. Ip (1985), 52 O.R. 289] by the Ontario Court of Appeal. Craig J.A. for the court held at pp. 203-5: The intent of R. 26(11) is to provide any party to an action with the means of obtaining the production and inspection of a document if the applicant is able to satisfy the judge that the document contains information which may relate to a matter in issue… A party applying for an order under R. 26(11) must satisfy the court that the application is not in the nature of a ‘fishing expedition’: Rhoades v. Occidental Life Ins. Co. of California[(1973), 3 W.W.R. 625 (B.C. C.A.)]. He must show that a person who is not a party to the action has a ‘document’ or ‘documents’ in his possession which relate to a matter in issue. The comments of Brett L.J. in Compagnie Financière du Pacifique v. Peruvian Guano Co. (1882), 11 Q.B.D. 55 at p. 63 (C.A.), as to what constitutes a document relating to a matter in question have been quoted by this court on several occasions: It seems to me that every document relates to the matters in question in the action, which not only would be evidence upon any issue, but also which, it is reasonable to suppose, contains information which may—not which must—either directly or indirectly enable the party requiring the affidavit either to advance his own cause or to damage the case of his adversary… It follows from this that an applicant need not show that a document is admissible in evidence at the trial as the condition of his obtaining an order under this rule. If a party seeking the order is able to satisfy the judge that the document, or information in a document, may relate to a matter in issue, the judge should make the order unless there are compelling reasons why he should not make it, e.g., the document is privileged…[Emphasis L'Heureux-Dubé J.'s.] In Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v. Wenzel, 2008 ABQB 574, 2008 CarswellAlta 1260, 461 A.R. 302, 96 Alta. L.R. (4th) 127, Justice Greckol, at pp. 140-141, gave the following summary of the law relating to Rule 209: 38 The following are the general principles which apply to Rule 209 applications: 1. Rule 209 is permissive, not mandatory, and the benefit of ordering production must equal the labour involved (W.A. Stevenson & J.E. Côté, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol. 2 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003) at 27–74). 2. The benefit must equal or surpass the harm done by prying into confidential papers (Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol. 2, p. 27–74; Ed Miller Sales and Rentals (1990)). 3. The Rule compelling non-parties to produce documents should not be used unless it can be shown that the documents are in existence and not available through other means. The Rule should only be used as a last resort (Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1990), 108 A.R. 161 (C.A.); Jahnke v. Wylle (1994), 162 A.R. 131, at para. 28 (C.A.)). 4. Rule 209 is not to be used for discovery of a non-party, but only for trial evidence (Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol. 2, p. 27–76; Ed Miller Sales & Rentals (1988)). 5. Rule 209 is not to be used as a fishing trip. It is to be used for specified documents only, which the court is satisfied exist (Esso Resources Canada Ltd.). 6. Although the Bank Act and provincial Evidence Acts have provisions for production and inspection of certain bank records, these provisions do not apply to a bank's internal memoranda and business papers (I.T.L. Industrial Ltd.). 39 In Ed Miller Sales and Rentals (1988), which involved a Rule 209 application brought by the plaintiff for an order directing its bank, a non-party to the action, to produce certain records, Wachowich J. (as he then was), accepted the approach taken by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Rhoades v. Occidental Life Ins. Co. of California, [1973] 3 W.W.R. 625. The court in that case adopted the “probable relevance” test for determining whether to order production of documents in the hands of a non-party to the action, with the following four caveats: 1. The rule should not be used as a fishing expedition to discover whether or not a person is in possession of a document. 2. The documents need not necessarily be admissible in evidence at trial. 3. The documents of which production is sought must be adequately described, but not necessarily so specifically that they can be picked out from any number of other documents. 4. The third party's objections to production must be considered, but are not determinative. 40 Wachowich J. added the condition that the Rule should not be used as a method of obtaining discovery of a person not a party to the action. In LC v. Office of the Child and Youth Advocate, 2024 ABCA 104, the Court said (at paragraph 20): [20] …An applicant under this rule must generally show the records sought exist; are under the control of the non-party; are relevant and material; and cannot be obtained from a party: CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v 801 Seventh Inc, 2023 ABCA 97 at para 27 [CNOOC]; Elhert v Sailer, 2023 ABCA 371 at para 23. While the chambers judge was satisfied of the relevance and materiality of the requested records, if they existed, he erred in ordering production without first being satisfied the remaining criteria were met. [21]… The chambers judge was satisfied some of the records existed….However, he held there was “no certainty that any” of the other records existed. He noted only that “it would be a logical assumption that there may” be some such additional records….Rule 5.13 is not to be used as a “fishing expedition” for non-party records…. 2. Test for Relevance In my view, the test of relevance emanating from rule 209 is dictated by the Rule itself. That rule states that if “any party has reason to believe that the document relates to the matters in issue” then it should be produced by the third party. ..... In my view, the test is not one of likely relevance but rather … it is one of whether or not the party requesting has reason to believe that the document relates to the matter in issue. Such reason to believe must be beyond something that raises a scintilla of a reason, but likelihood of relevancy can only be established if the party has actually seen the document. To conclude that likelihood of relevancy is required would be to render rule 209 meaningless. I draw support for this conclusion from the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Métropolitaine compagnie d'assurance-vie v. Frenette, Hôpital Jean-Talon et un autre, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 647 … wherein at p. 692 L'Heureux-Dubé, J., quotes from the decision of Brett, L.J., in Cie Financière du Pacifique v. Peruvian Guano Co. (1882), 11 Q.B.D. 55 at 63 (C.A.), as to what constitutes a document relating to a matter in question. She then states: It follows from this that an applicant need not show that a document is admissible in evidence at the trial as the condition of his obtaining an order under this rule. If a party seeking the order is able to satisfy the judge that the document, or information in a document, may relate to a matter in issue, the judge should make the order unless there are compelling reasons why he should not make it, e.g., the document is privileged. (emphasis L'Heureux-Dubé J.'s) In my view, the words “may relate” can be equated with “has reason to believe” and are a lesser requirement than the requirement of likely relevance. It is further my conclusion that in the matter before me the plaintiff has reason to believe that the documents requested relate to the matters in issue. That is, that they may relate to the matters in issue. Yellowbird (Next Friend of) v. Lytviak (1997), 210 A.R. 81 (Q.B.), at pp. 84-85, per Ritter J. 3. Procedure and claims of privilege In Cullihall v. Liyanage, 2016 ABQB 551, 2016 CarswellAlta 1943, the plaintiff (Cullihall) sued the defendant (Liyanage) for injuries suffered in a motor vehicle accident. During questioning, counsel for the defendant asked Mr. Cullihall to consent to a defence request of the plaintiff's former employer for Mr. Cullihall's employment file. The plaintiff refused, and took the position that the appropriate procedure was an application under Rule 5.13, and that under the Rule the non-party's records must first go to the plaintiff for assessment of relevance, materialty, and privilege. Master Mason disagreed. The learned Master said: 14 Rule 5.13 calls for a determination to be made by the court as to relevance and materiality. It is one of the pre-conditions to success under the rule. The manner in which that determination is arrived at must necessarily be determined in the context of the particular facts and pleadings in issue. 15 Here, we are dealing with records contained in employment files maintained by the Employers. The court can reasonably presume that there would be certain types of records maintained on such files. It is not difficult to discern their typical contents. 16 Mr. Cullihall did not suggest that the types of records sought did not exist or were not of the type typically maintained by an employer. He agreed that they likely contained relevant and material information. In the particular situation here, it may not be necessary to review the particular records for relevant and material contents. Rather, it may be appropriate to consider each type of record sought, and assess whether, as rule 5.13 contemplates, there is reason to believe that these contain information relevant and material to the matters in issue in the litigation. 17 As with its predecessor rule 209, rule 5.13(1)(b) continues to recognize that relevance and materiality need not be guaranteed in order for records to be directed to be produced by non-parties: see for example, Yellowbird v Lytviak (1997), 210 AR 81 (QB) at 84-85, citing Frenette v Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., [1992] 1 SCR 647. … 19 Against this backdrop of general principles relating to rule 5.13 applications, I turn now to Mr. Cullihall's specific submission that the proper procedure under rule 5.13 is to have the non-party records go first to the plaintiff for assessment of relevance, materiality and privilege. Who determines relevance, materiality and privilege under rule 5.13? 20 So long as Mr. Cullihall has not been and is not in control of the records, he is not required to disclose them: rule 5.6 and see for example, Brown v Malik, 2007 ABQB 270. Mr. Cullihall now wants to control the disclosure and production of records that he has steadfastly maintained are not within his control. 21 Mr. Cullihall relies on Phillips v Watson, 2007 ABCA 144 in support of his assertion that it is first the plaintiff who suggests what records of a non-party should be disclosed and produced. 22 It is not clear whether Phillips involved an application under rule 5.13's predecessor, rule 209. The Court of Appeal's reasons indicate that the plaintiff had the records in her possession, but did not want to produce them to the defendant on the basis of relevance. In any event, the decision does not stand for the proposition advanced by Mr. Cullihall. The ratio is that the court must determine the relevance and materiality of records before ordering production where there is an objection, and not delegate that determination to a party's physician (paragraph 9). … 27 Similarly here, I do not consider that every record on the Employers' files will be relevant and material to this litigation and that is not what the defendant asked for. For the most part, the defendant has identified and requested specific types of records, and set its requests in the context of this personal injury action in which the plaintiff has alleged past loss of income, and placed his future ability to work in issue. 28 The existence and typical contents of the records can generally be ascertained without difficulty. However, some of the defendant's requests appear to be overly broad and further submissions are needed to determine relevance and materiality. In my view, this approach is consistent with Phillips. … 30 Mr. Cullihall further argues that the records sought may potentially contain privileged information. 31 As with objections on the basis of relevance, the court is also obliged to consider objections on the basis of privilege under rule 5.13. In some cases, it may be necessary for the court to review the disputed documents in order to resolve the question of privilege. This too is consistent with Phillips. At paragraph 10 of its reasons, the Court of Appeal notes that the Supreme Court of Canada directed some flexibility in regard to the mode of determination, citing the reasons of McLachlin J (as she then was) in A.M. v Ryan, [1997] 1 SCR 157 at paragraph 39: In order to determine whether privilege should be accorded to a particular document or class of documents and, if so, what conditions should attach, the judge must consider the circumstances of the privilege alleged, the documents, and the case. While it is not essential in a civil case such as this that the judge examine every document, the court may do so if necessary to the inquiry. On the other hand, a judge does not necessarily err by proceeding on affidavit material indicating the nature of the information and its expected relevance without inspecting each document individually. The requirement that the court minutely examine numerous and lengthy documents may prove time-consuming, expensive and delay the resolution of the litigation. Where necessary to the proper determination of the claim for privilege, it must be undertaken. But I would not lay down an absolute rule that as a matter of law 32 However, the person objecting has to provide some cogent basis for expecting that privileged records may exist, and the basis of the claim to privilege. Mr. Cullihall's submissions do not do so in a sufficiently clear fashion. He indicated that “there is a first for everything.” The non-party records at issue in this application are contained in employment files, which do not raise obvious matters of privilege, as for example, a lawyer's file would. 33 I do not suggest that information subject to privilege in favor of an employee could never be found in an employer's file. However, Mr. Cullihall is asserting claims of privilege in this action which he has commenced to recover alleged damages for income loss and impairment of future ability to work. Further submissions are necessary in order for the defendant and the court to understand the basis of the privilege claimed. … 35 There is no serious dispute about the existence of typical records maintained by the non-party Employers, and their typical contents. Counsel for the plaintiff concedes that most of the records requested contain relevant and material information. The breadth of some of the defendant's requests and the lack of clarity in the plaintiff's claimed entitlement to privilege require further submissions in order for the court to make the necessary determinations. Court review of some of the records may or may not be necessary. 36 Counsel shall make an appointment to attend before me at a 2 pm sitting to make further submissions on relevance, materiality and privilege. No briefs are necessary. I encourage counsel to discuss the requested records and attempt to narrow their disputes in advance of the hearing. Counsel for Mr. Cullihall shall advise the court in advance of the hearing, what categories of records remain in dispute, along with the specific bases of objection and their grounds. Counsel may also consider that further affidavit evidence may assist the court in making the necessary determinations. In that event, counsel shall exchange the affidavits in advance of the hearing and provide courtesy copies to the Masters' office. 4. Crown Immunity Applies to Rule … I cannot agree that Crown immunity does not extend to R. 209 and 266 of the Alberta Rules of Court…Rutherford v. Swanson (1993), 9 Alta. L.R. (3d) 328 (Q.B.), at 333, per Bielby J. The same conclusion was arrived at by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Omega Techno Ltd. v. East Central Gas Co-op Ltd. (14th April 1979), as reproduced by Master Funduk in Barry v. Maertens-Poole (1992), 4 Alta. L.R. (3d) 330 (Master), at p. 331: Her Majesty is not bound by the rules in cases where she is not a party to the action. That was so held in Omega Techno Ltd. v. East Central Gas Co-op Ltd. (April 14, 1979), Docs. Calgary Appeal 11818, 11835 (Alta. C.A.). There the chambers judge had ordered the Crown, not a party to the action, to produce certain documents. This is what the court said on that point: Rule 209 has no application to the Crown when Her Majesty is not a party to the action. We are of the further view that with respect to R. 201 it has not been established that this is an action brought for the benefit of the Crown no matter how that rule is interpreted, and that therefore there is no requirement upon the Crown nor upon the East Central Gas Co-op to disclose any involvement that there may be on the part of the Crown in this litigation. With respect to the ‘Algas Report’ which the learned chambers judge ordered the Crown to produce and which direction we have already overruled, we note that this report is in the possession of the East Central Gas Co-op, they having received it from the Crown. In our opinion this report is not privileged in the hands of the East Central Gas Co-op and we order that it be produced by them. [emphasis Master Funduk's] However, Crown immunity arises from the function being performed, not just the office held by the person performing the function. In L'Heureux v. Unum Life Insurance Co. of America (1998), 222 A.R. 323 (Q.B.), a life insurer denied a beneficiary's accidental death benefit claim on the basis that the deceased's death was not accidental. In the resulting action brought by the beneficiary, the insurer sought production of records created by the R.C.M.P. in their capacity as medical investigators under the Fatality Inquiries Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. F-6. Murray J. said, at pp 325-26: Crown privilege or “public interest immunity” is a doctrine which restricts otherwise admissible and relevant evidence from admission in either civil or criminal proceedings if admission would be contrary to the public interest… In situations where public interest immunity is claimed, public interest competes against itself. On the one hand, public interest is served by the administration of justice which typically is furthered by the exchange of relevant information between litigants. On the other hand, the public interest is also tied to national security which embodies state secrets and, in some circumstances, government functioning and government documents. Angers, J., in Dufresne Construction Co. v. R., [1935] Ex. C.R 77, discussed the parameters of public interest at p. 88 where he stated: The privilege of exclusion of documents as evidence at the request of the Crown must not be extended beyond the requirements of public safety or convenience. Recently courts have adopted this standard which focuses more clearly on the balance of interests. After extensively canvassing the common law, Mr. Justice LaForest at p. 670 of Carey v. Ontario et al., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 637 … stated, in reference to Canadian Javelin Ltd., Re; Sparling et al. v. Smallwood, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686 … That case determines that Cabinet documents like other evidence must be disclosed unless such disclosure would interfere with the public interest. This standard was echoed by Miller, A.C.J.Q.B., in Leeds et al. v. Alberta (Minister of the Environment) et al. (1990), 69 D.L.R. (4th) 681 (Q.B.) … at p. 688: I have concluded from a reading of the leading decisions from the Supreme Court of Canada on the subject of public interest immunity … that the clear trend in Canada is towards the concept of extensive disclosure of Crown documents to assist in the fair administration of justice as opposed to any blanket concept of nondisclosure under the rubric of a public interest immunity concept. When analysing a claim of public interest immunity it is evident that principles such as public security and the administration of justice must be kept in mind. There is no dispute that the R.C.M.P. prima facie, enjoy public interest immunity. And at pp. 331-33: Members of the R.C.M.P., members of municipal police services and peace officers responsible for policing within Alberta pursuant to the Police Act are deemed to have the powers and duties of medical examiners' investigators pursuant to s. 9(1) of the Fatality Inquiries Act. The documents that are the subject of the present application were created by members of the Tofield R.C.M.P. acting as a medical examiners' investigator pursuant to the Fatality Inquiries Act. Thus at the relevant time there was no Federal Crown agency involvement. The Tofield R.C.M.P. members were conducting an investigation as directed by the Chief Medical Examiner and as such were agents of the Chief Medical Examiner. . . . . . The [Fatality Inquiries Act] in s. 31(1) goes on to say that once the investigation or public inquiry has been completed, and upon request from any adult next of kin or personal representative of the deceased, the Chief Medical Examiner shall send a report to the requesting party. . . . . . There is no differentiation made within the Fatality Inquiries Act between documents made by the R.C.M.P. acting as medical examiners' investigators and other parties acting as medical examiners' investigators. The same documents could be created by different parties under the Fatality Inquiries Act and be producible without question. To say that the documents created by medical examiners' investigators who are R.C.M.P. members are not producible for discovery is an absurd result. If there is can be no legitimate claim of public interest immunity for documents created by a medical examiners' investigator who is not a member of the R.C.M.P. there is no place for a claim of public interest immunity for the documents created by R.C.M.P. medical examiners' investigators. It must be remembered that public interest immunity does not rest indefinitely in any and all parties who feel themselves to be linked to the Crown. In circumstances such as this, the claim focuses upon the nature of the documents. A court must decide whether the public interest is better protected by the admission of the documents or by their exclusion. Regard must also be had to the administration of justice. Murray J. ordered production of the records. 5. Physicians' Notes One could use old Rule 209 in respect of physicians' notes. Since R. 5.13 is broader, it too should apply. It would be open to the defendant to apply under R. 209 to have the notes and records relating to the plaintiff in the physician's possession produced and copied. If the physician did not wish to produce such documents his objections could be considered by the court hearing the application. In the result, I have come to the conclusion that the notes and records in question are in the “power” of the plaintiff in the sense that it would be reasonable for her to request them from her physician. If the notes and records are not produced following such a request then an application would have to be made by the defendant pursuant to R. 209. Similar considerations apply to the notes and records in the possession of the physiotherapists. Price v. Labossiere (1985), 41 Alta. L.R. (2d) 253 (Q.B.), at 259, per Sinclair J. And Veit J. has stated: Rule 209 will answer the defendants' needs for production from the physicians of notes, X-rays and similar documents. Should the physician involved have a basis for refusing to produce the notes, X-rays and other documents, the physician's submissions can be assessed by the court … In summary on this issue, I am satisfied that: • R. 217 does not grant any privilege to the notes, records, X-rays, and other documents of a treating physician; • R. 217 does remove the privilege that would otherwise apply to medical reports obtained with a view to litigation; • where a claim for physical injuries is made, pre- and post-injury medical treatment is potentially relevant; • a party's entitlement to such pre- and post-injury records from a treating physician does not depend on that party's request for an independent medical examination; • the defendants may, within the framework of R. 209, obtain production of such medical records, notes, X-rays, and other documents without having requested an independent medical opinion. Kachkar v. Attwell (1990), 74 Alta. L.R. (2d) 63 at 66 and 68 (Q.B.). 6. Hospital Records One cannot use the rule for hospital records. The hospital refused to produce its records on the basis that: a) the required records are not compellable under R. 209; b) the hospital is prohibited from producing the records under s. 40 of the Hospitals Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. H-11 … Section 40(3) of the Hospitals Act states: (3) Information obtained from hospital records or from persons having access thereto shall be treated as private and confidential information in respect of any individual patient and shall be used solely for the purposes described in subsection (2) and the information shall not be published, released or disclosed in any manner that would be detrimental to the personal interests, reputation or privacy of a patient or the patient's attending physician or any other person providing diagnostic or treatment services to a patient … The plaintiff advanced the proposition that the hospital's admission records, (which would disclose the name of persons admitted to hospital) did not come within the protection of s. 40(3). He relied upon s. 40(1) which provides: 40. (1) The board of each approved hospital shall cause to be kept by the attending physician or any other person providing diagnostic or treatment services to a patient a record of the diagnostic and treatment services provided in respect of each patient in order to assist in providing a high standard of medical care. The plaintiff submits that only the record of diagnostic or treatment services is protected by the Act. I do not believe this interpretation takes into account the difference in wording between s. 40(1) and (3). What is protected by subs. (3) is “information from hospital records,” a term which is broader than “a record of the diagnostic and treatment services,” the term used in s. 40(1). A record of diagnostic or treatment services is part of—but does not comprise the whole of—the term “hospital records.” Support for this view is found in s. 12 of the Operation of Approved Hospitals Regulations (which applies to the Holy Cross Hospital, and is Alta. Reg. 146/71), which requires the hospital board to keep a record for each admission which shall “identify the patient.” The patient's identity is thereby made a part of the hospital's records which are protected by s. 40(3). I conclude, therefore, that hospital records, identifying by name persons admitted to hospital, constitute information which the hospital is prohibited from producing. Insofar as R. 209 is concerned, Steer J. in Unger v. Sun Alliance & London Assur. Co., [1978] 4 W.W.R. 759 … after concluding that there was, under the Hospitals Act, “an absolute prohibition against production of the documents,” said at p. 766: This being the position, it is my opinion that R. 209(1) does not authorize the court to make an order on behalf of the defendant directly against the board directing it or someone on its behalf to attend and produce the documents. Rule 209(1), albeit it has the effect of a statute, is a general rule only and must give way to the particular provisions of s. 35 [now s. 40]. I adopt this as a correct statement of the law in Alberta …Kiedynk v. John Doe (1991), 79 Alta. L.R. (2d) 72 (Q.B.), at 74-75, per Virtue J. 7. Privilege Claim Based on Author as Potential Witness Claims of privilege based on the retention of the author of the records as a potential witness cannot shield the records from production. It is not disputed that Dr. Hnatko's notes are relevant. The sole ground for the refusal to provide them is that at some point Dr. Hnatko was “retained” by counsel for the Defendants as an expert. Counsel for the Defendants says that Dr. Hnatko will be called by them as a witness. Relevant documents cannot be shielded from production merely by later “retaining” their author as an expert or later forming an intention to call the author as a witness. The fact that those documents might give a clue about the author's views and what his testimony is likely to be is irrelevant. That can be said of many documents prepared by people who are experts in a particular field. It is clear that the sole purpose or at least the dominant purpose in taking Jamie to Dr. Hnatko was to get help for Jamie. There is no “litigation privilege” attaching to that. All that would be privileged would be communications between Dr. Hnatko and counsel for the Defendants and any documents authored by Dr. Hnatko at counsel's request or because he had been retained by counsel as an expert. Dr. Hnatko's records of his “treatment” of Jamie (the usual physician's records) whether made before or after his retention as an expert are part of his general records about Jamie and are producible. The usual records that Dr. Hnatko would make regardless of his retention as the Defendants' expert are not made for the dominant purpose of litigation. Dr. Hnatko was retained by the female Defendant to provide psychiatric assistance to Jamie. His records on that must be produced. [emphasis Master Funduk's]Rachansky v. Walker (1993), 14 Alta. L.R. (3d) 195 (Master), at 199-200, per Master Funduk. 8. R. 5.13(2): Recovering the Expense of Producing Records In Janela v. Janela, 2017 ABQB 331, 2017 CarswellAlta 843, Justice Burrows said: 18 Counsel cited no authority as to the test the Court is to use in making the determination required by Rule 5.13(2) and I have not located any myself. 19 Rule 5.13(2) does not relate to the cost of opposing the application in which the production order was made. Whether the costs of appearing and opposing the application should be payable by the applicant to the party ordered to produce documents, even though they were not successful in their opposition to the application, is a matter to be raised before the judge who grants the order for production. 20 The February 28 consent order dealt with application costs. It provided that the Janela Corporations would not be required to pay costs. In my view, it is fair to interpret the consent order as intending that Ms. Janela, the successful party, would not pay costs either. Much of what the Janela Corporations now claim under Rule 5.13(2) is cost incurred in opposing the application and is therefore not properly the subject of an order under that Rule. 21 Rule 5.13(2) is intended to ensure that the non-party producing the records recovers the reasonable expense of producing them.
