Reg.
Application of Rule Rule 209 should not be used to permit discovery of a person not a party if it amounts to a fishing expedition.
The rule purports to deal with documents in the possession of a third person not a party to the action but does not relate to documents which are merely within the power and control of that person.
Wachowich, J., in Miller (Ed) Sales & Rentals Ltd. v.
Caterpillar Tractor Co. et al.
L.R.
(2d) 189, held at page 191: The British Columbia Court of Appeal in Rhoades v.

Occidental Life Insurance Company of California… set out the standard of ‘probable relevance’ as the basis test for determining whether to order production of documents in the hands of a person not a party to the action … The court attached four caveats to the ‘probable relevance’ test:
(1) the rule should not be used as a fishing expedition to discover whether or not a person is in possession of a document.
(2) the documents need not necessarily be admissible in evidence at trial.
(3) The documents of which production is sought must be adequately described, but not necessarily so specifically that they can be picked out from any number of other documents.
(4) the parties' objections to production must be considered, but are not determinative.
I accept this approach, with the additional condition that the rule cannot be used as a method of obtaining discovery of a person not a party to the action.
As Mr.
Justice Thompson of the Ontario High Court said in Markowitz v.
Toronto Transit Comm., [1965] 2 O.R.
215 at 217, when considering the Ontario equivalent of R.
209(1): Rule 349 was never intended to be used merely as a means of obtaining discovery from a stranger to the action, nor for exploratory purposes alone …Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
374 at 382 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1990), 74 Alta.
L.R.
In the Court of Appeal Esso decision, Stevenson J.A. said at pp.
L.R.
(2d)]: In my view this rule should not be used against a non-party unless it can be shown that the document is in existence and not available through other means; in this case, through a party.
If the document is relevant, and was in the possession of the plaintiffs, they are required to disclose its existence under R.
186, and may be asked about its disposition in the course of oral discovery.
I also agree with the Chief Justice that this form of production should be related to specific documents of at least probable relevance and is not a form of discovery of a non-party.
The Supreme Court of Canada in Frenette v.
Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., [1992] 1 S.C.R.
647, had occasion to comment upon the equivalent British Columbia rule.
The court spoke with approval of the B.C.
C.A.'s interpretation of the British Columbia rule.
It is fair to conclude that the court's comments are applicable to the Alberta rule.
At pp.

691-92 the Supreme Court of Canada said: Similarily, in British Columbia, rule 26(11) of the Supreme Court Rules provides: Where a document is in the possession or control of a person who is not a party, the court, on notice to the person and all other parties, may order production and inspection of the document or preparation of a certified copy that may be used instead of the original.

The manner in which a court should exercise its discretion under rule 26(11) as well as the scope of information which may be communicated to an applicant was spoken to by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Dufault v.
Stevens (1978), 6 B.C.L.R.
The British Columbia Court of Appeal took an approach analogous to the one chosen in Cook[Cook v.
289] by the Ontario Court of Appeal.
Craig J.A. for the court held at pp.
203-5: The intent of R.

26(11) is to provide any party to an action with the means of obtaining the production and inspection of a document if the applicant is able to satisfy the judge that the document contains information which may relate to a matter in issue… A party applying for an order under R.
26(11) must satisfy the court that the application is not in the nature of a ‘fishing expedition’: Rhoades v.
Occidental Life Ins.
Co. of California[(1973), 3 W.W.R.
He must show that a person who is not a party to the action has a ‘document’ or ‘documents’ in his possession which relate to a matter in issue.
The comments of Brett L.J. in Compagnie Financière du Pacifique v.
Peruvian Guano Co.
55 at p.

63 (C.A.), as to what constitutes a document relating to a matter in question have been quoted by this court on several occasions: It seems to me that every document relates to the matters in question in the action, which not only would be evidence upon any issue, but also which, it is reasonable to suppose, contains information which may—not which must—either directly or indirectly enable the party requiring the affidavit either to advance his own cause or to damage the case of his adversary… It follows from this that an applicant need not show that a document is admissible in evidence at the trial as the condition of his obtaining an order under this rule.

If a party seeking the order is able to satisfy the judge that the document, or information in a document, may relate to a matter in issue, the judge should make the order unless there are compelling reasons why he should not make it, e.g., the document is privileged…[Emphasis L'Heureux-Dubé J.'s.] In Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v.
Wenzel, 2008 ABQB 574, 2008 CarswellAlta 1260, 461 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 127, Justice Greckol, at pp.
140-141, gave the following summary of the law relating to Rule 209: 38 The following are the general principles which apply to Rule 209 applications: 1.
Rule 209 is permissive, not mandatory, and the benefit of ordering production must equal the labour involved (W.A.
Stevenson & J.E.
Côté, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol.
2 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003) at 27–74).
The benefit must equal or surpass the harm done by prying into confidential papers (Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol.
27–74; Ed Miller Sales and Rentals (1990)).
The Rule compelling non-parties to produce documents should not be used unless it can be shown that the documents are in existence and not available through other means.
The Rule should only be used as a last resort (Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
161 (C.A.); Jahnke v.
131, at para.
Rule 209 is not to be used for discovery of a non-party, but only for trial evidence (Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol.
27–76; Ed Miller Sales & Rentals (1988)).
Rule 209 is not to be used as a fishing trip.
It is to be used for specified documents only, which the court is satisfied exist (Esso Resources Canada Ltd.).

Although the Bank Act and provincial Evidence Acts have provisions for production and inspection of certain bank records, these provisions do not apply to a bank's internal memoranda and business papers (I.T.L.
Industrial Ltd.).

39 In Ed Miller Sales and Rentals (1988), which involved a Rule 209 application brought by the plaintiff for an order directing its bank, a non-party to the action, to produce certain records, Wachowich J.
(as he then was), accepted the approach taken by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Rhoades v.
Occidental Life Ins.
Co. of California, [1973] 3 W.W.R.
The court in that case adopted the “probable relevance” test for determining whether to order production of documents in the hands of a non-party to the action, with the following four caveats: 1.
The rule should not be used as a fishing expedition to discover whether or not a person is in possession of a document.
The documents need not necessarily be admissible in evidence at trial.
The documents of which production is sought must be adequately described, but not necessarily so specifically that they can be picked out from any number of other documents.
The third party's objections to production must be considered, but are not determinative.
40 Wachowich J. added the condition that the Rule should not be used as a method of obtaining discovery of a person not a party to the action.
In LC v.

Office of the Child and Youth Advocate, 2024 ABCA 104, the Court said (at paragraph 20): [20] …An applicant under this rule must generally show the records sought exist; are under the control of the non-party; are relevant and material; and cannot be obtained from a party: CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v 801 Seventh Inc, 2023 ABCA 97 at para 27 [CNOOC]
Elhert v Sailer, 2023 ABCA 371 at para 23.

While the chambers judge was satisfied of the relevance and materiality of the requested records, if they existed, he erred in ordering production without first being satisfied the remaining criteria were met.
[21]… The chambers judge was satisfied some of the records existed….However, he held there was “no certainty that any” of the other records existed.
He noted only that “it would be a logical assumption that there may” be some such additional records….Rule 5.13 is not to be used as a “fishing expedition” for non-party records….
Test for Relevance In my view, the test of relevance emanating from rule 209 is dictated by the Rule itself.
That rule states that if “any party has reason to believe that the document relates to the matters in issue” then it should be produced by the third party. .....
In my view, the test is not one of likely relevance but rather … it is one of whether or not the party requesting has reason to believe that the document relates to the matter in issue.
Such reason to believe must be beyond something that raises a scintilla of a reason, but likelihood of relevancy can only be established if the party has actually seen the document.
To conclude that likelihood of relevancy is required would be to render rule 209 meaningless.
I draw support for this conclusion from the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Métropolitaine compagnie d'assurance-vie v.
Frenette, Hôpital Jean-Talon et un autre, [1992] 1 S.C.R.
647 … wherein at p.
692 L'Heureux-Dubé, J., quotes from the decision of Brett, L.J., in Cie Financière du Pacifique v.
Peruvian Guano Co.
55 at 63 (C.A.), as to what constitutes a document relating to a matter in question.
She then states: It follows from this that an applicant need not show that a document is admissible in evidence at the trial as the condition of his obtaining an order under this rule.

If a party seeking the order is able to satisfy the judge that the document, or information in a document, may relate to a matter in issue, the judge should make the order unless there are compelling reasons why he should not make it, e.g., the document is privileged.
(emphasis L'Heureux-Dubé J.'s) In my view, the words “may relate” can be equated with “has reason to believe” and are a lesser requirement than the requirement of likely relevance.
It is further my conclusion that in the matter before me the plaintiff has reason to believe that the documents requested relate to the matters in issue.
That is, that they may relate to the matters in issue.
Yellowbird (Next Friend of) v.
Lytviak (1997), 210 A.R.
81 (Q.B.), at pp.
84-85, per Ritter J.
Procedure and claims of privilege In Cullihall v.
Liyanage, 2016 ABQB 551, 2016 CarswellAlta 1943, the plaintiff (Cullihall) sued the defendant (Liyanage) for injuries suffered in a motor vehicle accident.
During questioning, counsel for the defendant asked Mr.
Cullihall to consent to a defence request of the plaintiff's former employer for Mr.
Cullihall's employment file.

The plaintiff refused, and took the position that the appropriate procedure was an application under Rule 5.13, and that under the Rule the non-party's records must first go to the plaintiff for assessment of relevance, materialty, and privilege.
Master Mason disagreed.
The learned Master said: 14 Rule 5.13 calls for a determination to be made by the court as to relevance and materiality.
It is one of the pre-conditions to success under the rule.
The manner in which that determination is arrived at must necessarily be determined in the context of the particular facts and pleadings in issue.
15 Here, we are dealing with records contained in employment files maintained by the Employers.
The court can reasonably presume that there would be certain types of records maintained on such files.
It is not difficult to discern their typical contents.
16 Mr.
Cullihall did not suggest that the types of records sought did not exist or were not of the type typically maintained by an employer.
He agreed that they likely contained relevant and material information.
In the particular situation here, it may not be necessary to review the particular records for relevant and material contents.

Rather, it may be appropriate to consider each type of record sought, and assess whether, as rule 5.13 contemplates, there is reason to believe that these contain information relevant and material to the matters in issue in the litigation.

17 As with its predecessor rule 209, rule 5.13(1)(b) continues to recognize that relevance and materiality need not be guaranteed in order for records to be directed to be produced by non-parties: see for example, Yellowbird v Lytviak

(1997), 210 AR 81 (QB) at 84-85, citing Frenette v Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., [1992] 1 SCR 647. … 19 Against this backdrop of general principles relating to rule 5.13 applications, I turn now to Mr.
Cullihall's specific submission that the proper procedure under rule 5.13 is to have the non-party records go first to the plaintiff for assessment of relevance, materiality and privilege.
Who determines relevance, materiality and privilege under rule 5.13?
20 So long as Mr.
Cullihall has not been and is not in control of the records, he is not required to disclose them: rule 5.6 and see for example, Brown v Malik, 2007 ABQB 270.
Mr.
Cullihall now wants to control the disclosure and production of records that he has steadfastly maintained are not within his control.
21 Mr.
Cullihall relies on Phillips v Watson, 2007 ABCA 144 in support of his assertion that it is first the plaintiff who suggests what records of a non-party should be disclosed and produced.
22 It is not clear whether Phillips involved an application under rule 5.13's predecessor, rule 209.
The Court of Appeal's reasons indicate that the plaintiff had the records in her possession, but did not want to produce them to the defendant on the basis of relevance.
In any event, the decision does not stand for the proposition advanced by Mr.
Cullihall.

The ratio is that the court must determine the relevance and materiality of records before ordering production where there is an objection, and not delegate that determination to a party's physician (paragraph 9). … 27 Similarly here, I do not consider that every record on the Employers' files will be relevant and material to this litigation and that is not what the defendant asked for.

For the most part, the defendant has identified and requested specific types of records, and set its requests in the context of this personal injury action in which the plaintiff has alleged past loss of income, and placed his future ability to work in issue.
28 The existence and typical contents of the records can generally be ascertained without difficulty.
However, some of the defendant's requests appear to be overly broad and further submissions are needed to determine relevance and materiality.
In my view, this approach is consistent with Phillips. … 30 Mr.
Cullihall further argues that the records sought may potentially contain privileged information.
31 As with objections on the basis of relevance, the court is also obliged to consider objections on the basis of privilege under rule 5.13.
In some cases, it may be necessary for the court to review the disputed documents in order to resolve the question of privilege.
This too is consistent with Phillips.

At paragraph 10 of its reasons, the Court of Appeal notes that the Supreme Court of Canada directed some flexibility in regard to the mode of determination, citing the reasons of McLachlin J (as she then was) in A.M. v Ryan, [1997] 1 SCR 157 at paragraph 39: In order to determine whether privilege should be accorded to a particular document or class of documents and, if so, what conditions should attach, the judge must consider the circumstances of the privilege alleged, the documents, and the case.
While it is not essential in a civil case such as this that the judge examine every document, the court may do so if necessary to the inquiry.

On the other hand, a judge does not necessarily err by proceeding on affidavit material indicating the nature of the information and its expected relevance without inspecting each document individually.
The requirement that the court minutely examine numerous and lengthy documents may prove time-consuming, expensive and delay the resolution of the litigation.
Where necessary to the proper determination of the claim for privilege, it must be undertaken.

But I would not lay down an absolute rule that as a matter of law 32 However, the person objecting has to provide some cogent basis for expecting that privileged records may exist, and the basis of the claim to privilege.
Mr.
Cullihall's submissions do not do so in a sufficiently clear fashion.

He indicated that “there is a first for everything.” The non-party records at issue in this application are contained in employment files, which do not raise obvious matters of privilege, as for example, a lawyer's file would.
33 I do not suggest that information subject to privilege in favor of an employee could never be found in an employer's file.
However, Mr.
Cullihall is asserting claims of privilege in this action which he has commenced to recover alleged damages for income loss and impairment of future ability to work.

Further submissions are necessary in order for the defendant and the court to understand the basis of the privilege claimed. … 35 There is no serious dispute about the existence of typical records maintained by the non-party Employers, and their typical contents.
Counsel for the plaintiff concedes that most of the records requested contain relevant and material information.

The breadth of some of the defendant's requests and the lack of clarity in the plaintiff's claimed entitlement to privilege require further submissions in order for the court to make the necessary determinations.
Court review of some of the records may or may not be necessary.
36 Counsel shall make an appointment to attend before me at a 2 pm sitting to make further submissions on relevance, materiality and privilege.
No briefs are necessary.
I encourage counsel to discuss the requested records and attempt to narrow their disputes in advance of the hearing.
Counsel for Mr.
Cullihall shall advise the court in advance of the hearing, what categories of records remain in dispute, along with the specific bases of objection and their grounds.
Counsel may also consider that further affidavit evidence may assist the court in making the necessary determinations.
In that event, counsel shall exchange the affidavits in advance of the hearing and provide courtesy copies to the Masters' office.
Crown Immunity Applies to Rule … I cannot agree that Crown immunity does not extend to R.
209 and 266 of the Alberta Rules of Court…Rutherford v.
Swanson (1993), 9 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 328 (Q.B.), at 333, per Bielby J.
The same conclusion was arrived at by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Omega Techno Ltd. v.
East Central Gas Co-op Ltd.
(14th April 1979), as reproduced by Master Funduk in Barry v.
Maertens-Poole (1992), 4 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 330 (Master), at p.
331: Her Majesty is not bound by the rules in cases where she is not a party to the action.
That was so held in Omega Techno Ltd. v.
East Central Gas Co-op Ltd.
(April 14, 1979), Docs.
Calgary Appeal 11818, 11835 (Alta.
There the chambers judge had ordered the Crown, not a party to the action, to produce certain documents.
This is what the court said on that point: Rule 209 has no application to the Crown when Her Majesty is not a party to the action.
We are of the further view that with respect to R.

201 it has not been established that this is an action brought for the benefit of the Crown no matter how that rule is interpreted, and that therefore there is no requirement upon the Crown nor upon the East Central Gas Co-op to disclose any involvement that there may be on the part of the Crown in this litigation.

With respect to the ‘Algas Report’ which the learned chambers judge ordered the Crown to produce and which direction we have already overruled, we note that this report is in the possession of the East Central Gas Co-op, they having received it from the Crown.
In our opinion this report is not privileged in the hands of the East Central Gas Co-op and we order that it be produced by them.
[emphasis Master Funduk's] However, Crown immunity arises from the function being performed, not just the office held by the person performing the function.
In L'Heureux v.
Unum Life Insurance Co. of America (1998), 222 A.R.
323 (Q.B.), a life insurer denied a beneficiary's accidental death benefit claim on the basis that the deceased's death was not accidental.

In the resulting action brought by the beneficiary, the insurer sought production of records created by the R.C.M.P. in their capacity as medical investigators under the Fatality Inquiries Act, R.S.A.

Murray J. said, at pp 325-26: Crown privilege or “public interest immunity” is a doctrine which restricts otherwise admissible and relevant evidence from admission in either civil or criminal proceedings if admission would be contrary to the public interest… In situations where public interest immunity is claimed, public interest competes against itself.
On the one hand, public interest is served by the administration of justice which typically is furthered by the exchange of relevant information between litigants.
On the other hand, the public interest is also tied to national security which embodies state secrets and, in some circumstances, government functioning and government documents.
Angers, J., in Dufresne Construction Co. v.
C.R 77, discussed the parameters of public interest at p.
88 where he stated: The privilege of exclusion of documents as evidence at the request of the Crown must not be extended beyond the requirements of public safety or convenience.
Recently courts have adopted this standard which focuses more clearly on the balance of interests.
After extensively canvassing the common law, Mr.
Justice LaForest at p.
670 of Carey v.
Ontario et al., [1986] 2 S.C.R.
637 … stated, in reference to Canadian Javelin Ltd., Re; Sparling et al. v.
Smallwood, [1982] 2 S.C.R.
686 … That case determines that Cabinet documents like other evidence must be disclosed unless such disclosure would interfere with the public interest.
This standard was echoed by Miller, A.C.J.Q.B., in Leeds et al. v.
Alberta (Minister of the Environment) et al.

688: I have concluded from a reading of the leading decisions from the Supreme Court of Canada on the subject of public interest immunity … that the clear trend in Canada is towards the concept of extensive disclosure of Crown documents to assist in the fair administration of justice as opposed to any blanket concept of nondisclosure under the rubric of a public interest immunity concept.
When analysing a claim of public interest immunity it is evident that principles such as public security and the administration of justice must be kept in mind.
There is no dispute that the R.C.M.P. prima facie, enjoy public interest immunity.
And at pp.

331-33: Members of the R.C.M.P., members of municipal police services and peace officers responsible for policing within Alberta pursuant to the Police Act are deemed to have the powers and duties of medical examiners' investigators pursuant to s.
9(1) of the Fatality Inquiries Act.
The documents that are the subject of the present application were created by members of the Tofield R.C.M.P. acting as a medical examiners' investigator pursuant to the Fatality Inquiries Act.
Thus at the relevant time there was no Federal Crown agency involvement.
The Tofield R.C.M.P. members were conducting an investigation as directed by the Chief Medical Examiner and as such were agents of the Chief Medical Examiner. . . . . .
The [Fatality Inquiries Act] in s.

31(1) goes on to say that once the investigation or public inquiry has been completed, and upon request from any adult next of kin or personal representative of the deceased, the Chief Medical Examiner shall send a report to the requesting party. . . . . .

There is no differentiation made within the Fatality Inquiries Act between documents made by the R.C.M.P. acting as medical examiners' investigators and other parties acting as medical examiners' investigators.
The same documents could be created by different parties under the Fatality Inquiries Act and be producible without question.
To say that the documents created by medical examiners' investigators who are R.C.M.P. members are not producible for discovery is an absurd result.

If there is can be no legitimate claim of public interest immunity for documents created by a medical examiners' investigator who is not a member of the R.C.M.P. there is no place for a claim of public interest immunity for the documents created by R.C.M.P. medical examiners' investigators.
It must be remembered that public interest immunity does not rest indefinitely in any and all parties who feel themselves to be linked to the Crown.
In circumstances such as this, the claim focuses upon the nature of the documents.
A court must decide whether the public interest is better protected by the admission of the documents or by their exclusion.
Regard must also be had to the administration of justice.
Murray J. ordered production of the records.
Physicians' Notes One could use old Rule 209 in respect of physicians' notes.
Since R.
5.13 is broader, it too should apply.
It would be open to the defendant to apply under R.
209 to have the notes and records relating to the plaintiff in the physician's possession produced and copied.
If the physician did not wish to produce such documents his objections could be considered by the court hearing the application.

In the result, I have come to the conclusion that the notes and records in question are in the “power” of the plaintiff in the sense that it would be reasonable for her to request them from her physician.
If the notes and records are not produced following such a request then an application would have to be made by the defendant pursuant to R.
Similar considerations apply to the notes and records in the possession of the physiotherapists.
Price v.
Labossiere (1985), 41 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 253 (Q.B.), at 259, per Sinclair J.
And Veit J. has stated: Rule 209 will answer the defendants' needs for production from the physicians of notes, X-rays and similar documents.

Should the physician involved have a basis for refusing to produce the notes, X-rays and other documents, the physician's submissions can be assessed by the court … In summary on this issue, I am satisfied that: • R.
217 does not grant any privilege to the notes, records, X-rays, and other documents of a treating physician; • R.

217 does remove the privilege that would otherwise apply to medical reports obtained with a view to litigation; • where a claim for physical injuries is made, pre- and post-injury medical treatment is potentially relevant; • a party's entitlement to such pre- and post-injury records from a treating physician does not depend on that party's request for an independent medical examination; • the defendants may, within the framework of R.
209, obtain production of such medical records, notes, X-rays, and other documents without having requested an independent medical opinion.
Kachkar v.
Attwell (1990), 74 Alta.
L.R.
Hospital Records One cannot use the rule for hospital records.
The hospital refused to produce its records on the basis that: a) the required records are not compellable under R.
209; b) the hospital is prohibited from producing the records under s.
40 of the Hospitals Act, R.S.A.
H-11 … Section 40(3) of the Hospitals Act states:

(3) Information obtained from hospital records or from persons having access thereto shall be treated as private and confidential information in respect of any individual patient and shall be used solely for the purposes described in subsection

(2) and the information shall not be published, released or disclosed in any manner that would be detrimental to the personal interests, reputation or privacy of a patient or the patient's attending physician or any other person providing diagnostic or treatment services to a patient … The plaintiff advanced the proposition that the hospital's admission records, (which would disclose the name of persons admitted to hospital) did not come within the protection of s.
He relied upon s.
40(1) which provides: 40.

(1) The board of each approved hospital shall cause to be kept by the attending physician or any other person providing diagnostic or treatment services to a patient a record of the diagnostic and treatment services provided in respect of each patient in order to assist in providing a high standard of medical care.
The plaintiff submits that only the record of diagnostic or treatment services is protected by the Act.
I do not believe this interpretation takes into account the difference in wording between s.
What is protected by subs.
(3) is “information from hospital records,” a term which is broader than “a record of the diagnostic and treatment services,” the term used in s.
A record of diagnostic or treatment services is part of—but does not comprise the whole of—the term “hospital records.” Support for this view is found in s.
12 of the Operation of Approved Hospitals Regulations (which applies to the Holy Cross Hospital, and is Alta.
Reg.

146/71), which requires the hospital board to keep a record for each admission which shall “identify the patient.” The patient's identity is thereby made a part of the hospital's records which are protected by s.
I conclude, therefore, that hospital records, identifying by name persons admitted to hospital, constitute information which the hospital is prohibited from producing.
Insofar as R.
209 is concerned, Steer J. in Unger v.
Sun Alliance & London Assur.
759 … after concluding that there was, under the Hospitals Act, “an absolute prohibition against production of the documents,” said at p.
766: This being the position, it is my opinion that R.
209(1) does not authorize the court to make an order on behalf of the defendant directly against the board directing it or someone on its behalf to attend and produce the documents.
Rule 209(1), albeit it has the effect of a statute, is a general rule only and must give way to the particular provisions of s.
35 [now s.
I adopt this as a correct statement of the law in Alberta …Kiedynk v.
John Doe (1991), 79 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 72 (Q.B.), at 74-75, per Virtue J.
Privilege Claim Based on Author as Potential Witness Claims of privilege based on the retention of the author of the records as a potential witness cannot shield the records from production.
It is not disputed that Dr.
Hnatko's notes are relevant.
The sole ground for the refusal to provide them is that at some point Dr.
Hnatko was “retained” by counsel for the Defendants as an expert.
Counsel for the Defendants says that Dr.
Hnatko will be called by them as a witness.
Relevant documents cannot be shielded from production merely by later “retaining” their author as an expert or later forming an intention to call the author as a witness.
The fact that those documents might give a clue about the author's views and what his testimony is likely to be is irrelevant.
That can be said of many documents prepared by people who are experts in a particular field.
It is clear that the sole purpose or at least the dominant purpose in taking Jamie to Dr.
Hnatko was to get help for Jamie.
There is no “litigation privilege” attaching to that.
All that would be privileged would be communications between Dr.
Hnatko and counsel for the Defendants and any documents authored by Dr.
Hnatko at counsel's request or because he had been retained by counsel as an expert.
Dr.
Hnatko's records of his “treatment” of Jamie (the usual physician's records) whether made before or after his retention as an expert are part of his general records about Jamie and are producible.
The usual records that Dr.
Hnatko would make regardless of his retention as the Defendants' expert are not made for the dominant purpose of litigation.
Dr.
Hnatko was retained by the female Defendant to provide psychiatric assistance to Jamie.
His records on that must be produced.
[emphasis Master Funduk's]Rachansky v.
Walker (1993), 14 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 195 (Master), at 199-200, per Master Funduk.
R.
5.13(2): Recovering the Expense of Producing Records In Janela v.

Janela, 2017 ABQB 331, 2017 CarswellAlta 843, Justice Burrows said: 18 Counsel cited no authority as to the test the Court is to use in making the determination required by Rule 5.13(2) and I have not located any myself.
19 Rule 5.13(2) does not relate to the cost of opposing the application in which the production order was made.

Whether the costs of appearing and opposing the application should be payable by the applicant to the party ordered to produce documents, even though they were not successful in their opposition to the application, is a matter to be raised before the judge who grants the order for production.
20 The February 28 consent order dealt with application costs.
It provided that the Janela Corporations would not be required to pay costs.
In my view, it is fair to interpret the consent order as intending that Ms.
Janela, the successful party, would not pay costs either.
Much of what the Janela Corporations now claim under Rule 5.13(2) is cost incurred in opposing the application and is therefore not properly the subject of an order under that Rule.
21 Rule 5.13(2) is intended to ensure that the non-party producing the records recovers the reasonable expense of producing them.

paragraphs.text: (1) Every party is entitled, with respect to a record that is relevant and material and that is under the control of another party, to all of the following: (a) to inspect the record on one or more occasions on making a written request to do so; (b) to receive a copy of the record on making a written request for the copy and paying reasonable copying expenses; (c) to make copies of the record when it is produced. (2) This rule does not apply to a record for which a claim of privilege is made unless the Court orders the record to be produced for inspection. (3) The Court or a party to an action who receives a computer-generated document that was filed with the court clerk may request the person filing that document or causing it to be issued to provide a copy of it in an electronic format.

Canada (Attorney General), 2000 ABQB 536, 2000 CarswellAlta 853, 269 A.R. 97, 83 Alta. L.R. (3d) 346, Burrows J. summarized the law regarding confidentiality of information obtained through the discovery process. At pp. 348-350, his Lordship said: That an implied undertaking applies to information obtained through the discovery processes available in civil litigation in this court is firmly established. Simply by obtaining information through the discovery process a litigant and the litigant's counsel become subject to an undertaking not to use the information so obtained for any purpose other than the action. The undertaking is to the court. A breach is a contempt of court. … It is also recognized that a person subject to the implied undertaking may apply to the court for relief from the undertaking—in effect for leave to use the information obtained through the discovery process for some purpose outside the action in which it was obtained. … The requirement that a litigant submit to discovery is an intrusion on the litigant's interest in privacy and the confidentiality of private information. That intrusion is permitted in order to ensure that there is full disclosure, and therefore a better chance of a just result, in the action in which the discovery occurs. The implied undertaking exists to limit the effect of the intrusion by ensuring that the information is used only for the purpose for which the litigant is obliged to provide it. Relieving the litigant who has received the discovery information from the undertaking upsets the balance the undertaking is intended to create. It should only be done where the interest sought to be advanced through the use of the otherwise confidential discovery information outweighs the litigant's privacy and confidentiality interests. The same interests which are brought into balance by the undertaking must be reassessed to determine which has greater significance. If disclosing a litigant's privacy interest outweighs the interest sought to be served by disclosure, the undertaking should be kept in place. If the interest to be served by disclosure is more significant, relief from the undertaking should be granted. Wachowich J. (as he then was) has said: Rule 189 [now R. 188] of the Alberta Rules of Court sets out the defendant's rights of access to C.C.B.'s documents, and prima facie the rule makes no allowance for the detailed restrictions on access which the liquidator wishes to impose. The liquidator's proposal would not outright deny access to the documents, but it would require written undertakings of confidentiality from the defendants and their counsel before the provision of particulars. The proposal would require similar undertakings to be given by any other persons, such as experts or clerking staff, who are provided with a copy of the documents. As well, a detailed procedure for obtaining access, inspection and copies of the documents has also been provided by the applicant. Re Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidiation) (1990), 106 A.R. 205 (Q.B.), at 207, per Wachowich J. There must be some unusual risk to justify the court in imposing restrictions additional to those imposed by law. … the law in Alberta will imply the undertaking that information acquired through the discovery process shall not be used for any purpose ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit. While each case must be decided on its own facts, I found that the court's application of the principles would naturally result in three broad categories of cases. To borrow my own words in Ed Miller, supra, at 301: In the majority of cases, the implied undertaking is sufficient. The next level of cases is where the Court may require a formal undertaking by the party or their counsel not to misuse the information. Finally, the extreme position is composed of a ‘small hard core of cases’ where additional precautions are necessary to ensure no abuse of the discovery process … While I accept that certain particulars concerning C.C.B.'s former and present cusotmers may be confidential in nature, this fact alone is insufficient reason to require anything more explicit from the defendants and their counsel than the undertakings which have already been implied at law. As well, the defendant's accountants also already owe a professional duty of confidentiality, as attested to by the affidavit of John Bathurst, C.A. In the words of Anderson J., when presented with the same issue in the recent case of Reichmann et al. v. Toronto Life Publishing Co. et al. (1988), 28 C.P.C. (2d) 11, at 24: I am satisfied that the implied undertaking is a sufficient safeguard for the plaintiffs against any risk reasonably to be anticipated on the material. The defendants will use any information or documents with knowledge of the implied undertaking, which will no doubt dictate a prudent course. If the defendants are in any doubt about any prospective use of any material, they have always open to them the remedy of a motion to exempt such material from the implied undertaking. In the event of any objectionable use, the plaintiffs always have open to them the remedy of injunction. In the existing circumstances, and at the present time, I see no need for the order sought. … The plaintiff liquidator's second application for an Order restricting access to and requiring confidentiality for their discovery documents is granted only to the extent that an express undertaking will be required from the clerical staff involved. The sheer number and complexity of documents involved has convinced me that considerations of confidentiality will justify obtaining such undertakings from what will necessarily be a large clerical network. The undertakings implied by law from the parties and professional people in this action otherwise provide sufficient protection for the plaintiffs. Re Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidation) (1990), 106 A.R. 205 at 208-209 (Q.B.). And Mr. Justice Lutz has said: It is my view that the law in Alberta does recognize the implied undertaking. Further, in keeping with the broadening right of the discovery process, this implied undertaking confines all information arising from the discovery process, whether it is oral or documentary evidence, to the lawsuit at hand. The undertaking by the solicitor and the parties is to maintain all information confidential in that it is not to be used for any collateral, ulterior or improper purpose. The purpose of the implied undertaking “is to ensure full and complete disclosure while maintaining the confidentiality of a private process”… The following principles are summarized from the cases, and set out below as being applicable in Alberta: 1. The implied undertaking which is to the court, attaches to all discovery information whether obtained orally or in the form of documents … 2. Additionally, a non-disclosure order may be sought from the court in cases where there are special circumstances, such as patent processes, trade mark rights, sensitive or personal information, or in highly competitive industries … In these cases, a specific order could be sought to have the information sealed. The test for this non-disclosure order is that of a “real risk”… 3. There is also a right to apply to the court to remove the document or other evidence in whole or in part from the implied undertaking or sealing order for use in other proceedings. For example, to test the credibility of a witness where that witness has testified before in a proceeding in respect of the same subject matter and it can be shown that the evidence in this proceeding is or appears to be contrary thereto: see Alberta Evidence Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. A-21, ss. 1(c) and 26. Such application would also cover the possible situation where the discovery discloses fraudulent or criminal conduct. However, notably, “The public interest in investigating possible crimes is not per se a sufficient ground to relieve counsel of his or her implied undertaking to keep such information private”… 4. Counsel, as officers of the court, have a duty not to disclose or use oral evidence or documents outside the subject proceedings, so as to, at all times, honour the implied undertaking. 5. Counsel, as officers of the court who are not directly involved or involved at all in the proceeding have a similar obligation. 6. So as to not devalue the implied undertaking and in special circumstances, transcripts and copies of documents may be made available to parties outside the proceedings only with leave of the court. Without leave, no use shall be made of the same by any person who by the discovery or trial process comes into such information or documents. 7. The implied undertaking and non-disclosure orders continue after the use of the information in court and thereafter except with leave of the court. Wirth Ltd. v. Acadia Pipe & Supply Corp. (1991), 79 Alta. L.R. (2d) 345 at 361-62 (Q.B.). Madam Justice Coutu considered the matter in Ochitwa v. Bombino (1997), 56 Alta. L.R. (3d) 37 (Q.B.). Her Ladyship agreed with Lutz J.'s comments in Wirth and further said, at pp. 42-44: It is clear that Alberta law imposes upon litigants an implied undertaking not to use information or documents for any purpose ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit in which they are discovered. . . . . . If a party requesting the information to be produced later attempts to use the information for the purposes of another lawsuit, as against the parties who produced the information, the courts have held that that is in breach of the implied undertaking rule and have stayed the action as being an abuse of process… In the present case, the Plaintiff submits that the implied undertaking rule should cover only information that the receiving party could not otherwise have obtained by legitimate means independent of the litigation process and submits that the obligation is in favour of the producing party only, not third parties. There is no necessity for narrowing the scope of the implied undertaking rule. I agree with the broad rule that Lutz, J. set out, that is, the implied undertaking by the solicitors and the parties to an action is to maintain all information arising from the discovery process confidential in that it is not to be used for any collateral or ulterior purpose without leave of the court. A party can apply to the court to remove the document or evidence in whole or in part from the implied undertaking. The court has the discretion to review each particular case and make a determination whether it is in the public interest to remove the document or other evidence from the implied undertaking. The fact that the information could have been obtained independent of the litigation process or that a third party is involved may be factors influencing a court to exercise its discretion to give relief from the undertaking. There should not be a rigid rule that if either of these conditions existed the implied undertaking rule would not be applicable. In the Carbone decision [Carbone v. De La Rocha (1993), 13 O.R. (3d) 355 (Ont. Gen. Div.)] at page 367 the Court commented that the implied undertaking rule is still being developed: In summary, then, although the rule was initially expressed in terms of maintaining private proprietary interest and confidentiality, its ultimate foundation rests in the necessity to preserve the integrity of a process which: (a) encourages and requires full disclosure in respect to the issues being litigated; and (b) consequently promotes a just conclusion to the existing dispute, either by agreed settlement of the parties or the adjudication of the Court. Whether and when the court will permit some collateral use of discovered information has not yet been fully or clearly explored. Perhaps the variety of human affairs defies the development of comprehensive guidelines. While the courts are sensitive to the intrusion occasioned to individual parties who are compelled to disclose, the sensitivity is secondary to the concern that such intrusion be strictly limited to the purpose of the litigation, less [sic] the system which depends upon full disclosure be undermined by purposes or motives outside the confines of the immediate process. The individual interests are to be weighed against the public interests in an efficient and fair system of justice. It is also clear that the courts do not wish to be perceived as instruments of purposes ulterior to the immediate issue they are being asked to resolve. (emphasis Coutu J.'s) In Law Society (Alberta) v. Randhawa (1996), 39 Alta. L.R. (3d) 226 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice LoVecchio considered the following issue arising from Wirth: does the implied undertaking of all lawyers to the court to use transcripts of examinations for discovery only for the purposes of the litigation in which they were taken, unless leave of the court is obtained, apply to lawyers acting for the Law Society who come into possession of those transcipts during the course of a bona fide Law Society investigation of one of its members? At pp. 228-29, his Lordship said: Should Wirth be interpreted as an absolute rule with the incumbent corollary that relief from the rule may only be obtained by leave of the Court or should the rule be considered more limited and therefore not applicable in certain circumstances? Without in any way stating whether there should be any other exceptions, for the reasons which follow, in my view the rule should not be construed as absolute in so far as it relates to the self regulatory matters contemplated by the Legal Profession Act. At p. 231, he concluded: Having regard for the above, I do not believe I do any disservice to the logic or the wisdom of the Lutz, J. decision in Wirth by limiting the scope of the implied undertaking (so as not to require leave of the Court) when we are dealing with a Law Society investigation of one of its members for misconduct. In a much different fact situation, the use of discovery transcripts was also addressed by the Court of Appeal. In U.N.A. v. Alberta Children's Hospital (1996), 40 Alta. L.R. (3d) 128, a nurse was dismissed from her employment due to an inability to perform her duties as a result of a motor vehicle accident. The nurse grieved her dismissal, and, in the grievance proceedings, the hospital requested transcripts from the accident litigation discoveries. The issue was what, if any, implied undertakings attached to the produced transcripts. At pp. 129-30, the court said: The grievor contended that she was bound by an implied undertaking not to disclose what was said on examination for discovery, and that the court should not relieve against that … The first issue is whether the implied undertaking binds or affects the grievor. We know of no authority which says that the implied undertaking applies to her. It is customarily expressed as an undertaking by a party to litigation who receives documents or information by the discovery process not to use what he or she receives for collateral purposes, without leave of the court. Nor would the usual rationale expressed for the undertaking apply to a party who gives information on discovery as the grievor did. Nor is this a case where the respondent hospital seeks to use a discovery transcript which it got from the former litigation opponents of the grievor, or indeed from any non-party. The respondent hospital seeks the transcripts from the grievor herself. However, we do not wish to foreclose discussion of that interesting topic in another case. It is possible that other rationales do exist for creating some restriction on the use which non-parties may make of discovery transcripts, or for giving the witness on discovery some kind of privacy for some or all parts of the transcript of his or her answers on discovery. There is much which might be said on both sides on such an issue. There are many different factual situations which might arise, not all of them easy to forsee now. What is relevant in one suit can be irrelevant in another, and indirectly relevant in a third. What is disclosed in one suit may be harmless in another, and very harmful or embarrassing in a third. In Casavant v. Alberta Co-op Taxi Line Ltd. (1996), 41 Alta. L.R. (3d) 425 (Master), Master Funduk discussed the undertaking, to whom it is made, and the remedy for its breach. At pp. 426-28 the learned Master said: Litigants are compelled by the court to discover and produce all documents which are or have been in their possession or power relating to all matters or questions in the lawsuit: Rules 186 and 189. Litigants are compelled by the court to submit to an oral examination by any litigant adverse in interest: Rule 200. Because of that compulsion the court says that documents obtained through the discovery process and information obtained from the oral examinations shall be used by the adverse litigants only for the purposes of the lawsuit. The common statement is that what is obtained through the discovery process shall not be used for any purpose which is ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit … The court imposes an implied undertaking on the litigants that they will not use that information except for purposes related to the lawsuit. It is done by the court as part of its inherent jurisidiction to control its own practice … Like coins, undertakings are not one sided. The undertaking is by the litigant. Who is it given to? Alterskye v. Scott, [1948] 1 All E.R. 469 Ch. D., says that a breach of the undertaking is contempt of court … That implies that the undertaking is given to the court, not the adverse litigant. The learned Master then quoted from Alterskye and said: I do not read the last phrase to mean that the aggrieved litigant can sue for damages. The aggrieved litigant can ask the court to expressly order the other litigant to stop the breach, if it is continuing. That should be done by an application in the existing lawsuit because it relates to the conduct of the lawsuit… Harman[Home Office v. Harman, [1983] A.C. 280 (H.L.)]… says that the implied undertaking is to the court. Breach of that undertaking is a contempt of court. Lord Diplock says that such a contempt of court would be civil, and the court would deal with it only on a motion by the other litigant. Lord Keith of Kinkel says that the implied undertaking is owed not to the owner of the documents but to the court, and the function of the court in seeing that the obligation is observed is directed to the maintenance of the proper administration of justice and not to the enforcement of the law relating to confidentiality. Lord Scarman says that the obligation is formulated as arising from an undertaking exacted by the court from the party and his solicitor to whom the documents are disclosed. Breach of the obligation is a contempt of court… There is no cause of action for breach of the implied undertaking. The remedy is to apply to have the employer held in contempt of court. Also see the annotation: “Testimony in Other Proceedings” under R. 187.1. Also see the annotation “Implied Undertaking Regarding Confidentiality” under R. 200. 2. Anton Piller Orders In Catalyst Partners Inc. v. Meridian Packaging Ltd., 2007 ABCA 201, 2007 CarswellAlta 816, 417 A.R. 7, 76 Alta. L.R. (4th) 264, the Court gave the following explanation of Anton Piller orders (at pp. 265-266): 5 The production of records is a normal step in all civil litigation. Once pleadings are closed, each party is required to discover under oath all the relevant and material documents in its possession. The rules on the discovery of records presume a considerable amount of good faith on the part of the litigants. They presume that the litigants will not conceal or neglect to discover any relevant and material documents, and they also therefore assume that the litigants will not actually destroy any of those documents. 6 The Anton Piller order is an extraordinary remedy that displaces the normal rules on discovery of records. Anton Piller orders are applied for ex-parte, usually before the defendant even knows that an action has been commenced. The orders enable the plaintiff to attend at the premises of the defendant, without notice, and take possession of the records of the defendant. They are highly intrusive orders, made without giving the defendant the opportunity to respond to the allegations, and are therefore subject to a number of procedural limitations designed to protect the defendant. Anton Piller orders are extraordinary orders, and should not be routinely granted: Celanese Canada Inc. v. Murray Demolition Corp., [2006] 2 S.C.R. 189, 2006 SCC 36. They are limited to extreme cases. 7 Celanese Canada at para. 35 sets out four essential conditions for the granting of an Anton Piller order: a) The plaintiff must demonstrate a strong prima facie case; b) The damage to the plaintiff of the defendant's alleged misconduct must be very serious; c) There must be convincing evidence that the defendant has in its possession incriminating documents or things; and d) It must be shown that there is a real possibility that the defendant may destroy such material before the discovery process can do its work. Since the raison d'etre of an Anton Piller order is to preserve documents that might otherwise be destroyed, the fourth criterion is of central importance. 8 As mentioned, Anton Piller orders are always granted ex-parte. The initial ex-parte order is frequently followed by a second review by the court, during which the defendant seeks to set aside the Anton Piller order, and the plaintiff seeks to have the order confirmed and the seized documents released to it. By the time of the second stage the defendant will have had an opportunity to file evidence, the plaintiff may well have supplemented its evidence, and there will likely have been cross-examination on the various affidavits. It follows that the evidence at the second de novo stage of the process might well be different than that available on the original ex-parte application. 3. Electronic Records In Questor Technology Inc v. Stagg, 2022 ABQB 578, 2022 CarswellAlta 2372, Justice D. Nixon discussed production of records which exist in multiple formats: [114] Where records exist in multiple formats, including their native format, they must be produced: Bard v Canadian Natural Resources, 2016 ABQB 267 at para 96 [Bard], citing 2038724 Ontario Ltd v Quizno's Canada Restaurant Corp, 2012 ONSC 6549 at paras 128–131[Quizno's]. The production of documents in non-native format is not as meaningful and does not permit the plaintiff to take full advantage of available technology as documents available in their native format: Gamble v MGI Securities, 2011 ONSC 2705 at para 22. [115] In Bard, the Court considered whether it should order a party to produce records in a format importable into Microsoft Excel: Bard at paras 96–115. The party resisting disclosure argued that it did not keep records in this file format and that it would be significantly costly for it to produce the files: Bard paras 101–104. Notwithstanding the arguments of the resisting party in Bard, the Court in that case ordered the native files to be created and produced: Bard at para 125. In doing so, the Court noted the importance of usable files in resolving disputes: Usability is as much a concern for a litigant as it is for the Court. Producing records in an unusable format undermines procedural fairness and just results. It does not help to narrow the issues in dispute, and not only impairs the plaintiff's ability to prove its case, but also threatens the Court's ability to understand the evidence put before it …: Bard at para 115. … [121] Metadata is a producible record where relevant and material: Spar at para 75-76. Where the timing of the treatment of records, including when they were modified, and the dates and tracking routes of emails are at issue in litigation, metadata will be producible: Spar at para 76. In Spar Aerospace Ltd. v. Aerowerks Engineering Inc., 2007 ABQB 543, 2007 CarswellAlta 1156, 428 A.R. 84, 80 Alta. L.R. (4th) 123; affirmed 2008 ABCA 47, 2008 CarswellAlta 143, 85 Alta. L.R. (4th) 14, Veit J. made the following general comment in respect of the production of electronic records (at p. 129 [80 Alta. L.R. (4th) 123]): … the production of electronic records should be produced electronically; hence, the party to whom the records are produced is entitled to all passwords, operating systems and system-related files to allow real access to the produced material. Her Ladyship then made these specific comments (at pp. 141-142): 68 The defendants are required to provide to Spar all passwords, systems and software necessary to access the records produced. 69 Here, the defendants have provided approximately 1.2 gigabytes of information, much of which is password protected and therefore inaccessible to Spar. 70 It was always the case that production included an obligation to provide all technical information necessary to allow the receiving party to access the production: Canadian Engineering and Surveys (Yukon) Limited. 71 That general principle carries over to electronic disclosure. Moreover, it is obvious that the defendants should produce their electronic records electronically: not only is hard copy production considerably more expensive, but it is also less searchable and is inferior because it does not retain potentially critical meta- data such as when and by whom a record was created or amended: Cholakis. In order to access the electronic disclosure, it is obvious that a receiving party requires from the producing party whatever passwords and other systems necessary in order to constitute real disclosure. d) Must unprocessed records be produced? 72 The defendants must produce their electronic records in a meaningful way. Here the electronic records provided have not been processed for export into an electronic document database program. 73 The principles of meaningful disclosure are the same, whether disclosure is made by electronic or paper means: Wilson, Prism Hospital Software Inc., Nicolardi. e) Must metadata be produced? 74 In the circumstances here, the defendants must produce their metadata. 75 Metada is a record: Desgagne. 76 While metada presumably need not be produced in most situations, because it is irrelevant to know, for example, when a document was printed, the production of such records is material and relevant here where the pleadings disclose that the identity of the author of electronic records, the timing of the treatment of those records—including if and when they were modified, the dates and tracking routes of e-mail, are all potentially at the very core of the issues that are raised in the litigation. 5. Must the hard drives be produced? 77 Spar has proven its entitlement to access to the defendants' hard drives and is entitled to immediate access to them. 78 It goes without saying, that access to the opponent's hard drives will not always be granted by a court: Baldwin Janzen, Ireland.… 4. Translation of Documents What is before me is whether a litigant has complied if he undertakes to produce documents and he has in fact produced them but they are in a different language than the opposite party expected. They may well be in a different language than the producing party expected as well, and it is almost implicit from the context of this application that that is what happened here. It may well be that Mr. Erler would not have undertaken to produce those documents if he knew they were in the German language and was required to translate them. In my view the proper approach is to ask who wants the documents and for whose benefit are they produced. The plaintiff has not suggested it needs the documents or that it will be relying on them. The defendants are the ones who want the documents and obviously they have no idea whether they will be relying on them until they know the content of those documents … If the defendants want to see what these documents are all about they will have to accept the time and cost risks inherent in translating them. In my view the plaintiff has complied with the undertakings. Jasper Millwork Ltd. v. Borden Co. (1996), 47 Alta. L.R. (3d) 181 (Master), at 183, per Master Breitkreuz. 5. The Imposition of Conditions Will Be Unusual In B.E. Kennedy Design Ltd. v. Kibo Group Inc., 2000 ABQB 429, 2000 CarswellAlta 659, 269 A.R. 156; additional reasons at 2001 ABQB 32, 2001 CarswellAlta 2630, 304 A.R. 2, an individual defendant wanted to inspect the plaintiff's records pursuant to Rule 193. The plaintiff wanted the court to impose a condition that the defendant's lawyer accompany the defendant during the inspection. The Court refused to do so. Veit, J. said, at pp. 157-158: A party has a right to inspect the documents produced for discovery by parties opposite; that right should only be restricted where circumstances warrant. At this pre-trial stage, each party has an obligation to protect their own documents, and indeed has a self-interest in doing so. The documents that are produced on discovery are not necessarily going to be exhibits at trial; therefore, the court does not yet have an obligation to safeguard these documents. The exercise of the right to inspection should not be limited by imposing a financial burden on the inspecting party. The Rule points the way to the right result in this matter: if a party wants a copy of a document, that copy will be made at the inspecting party's expense. However, the mere inspection of the documents is a right, not something which the inspecting party must pay for. The producing party can impose a framework on the inspection which will promote the security of the documents. For example, the producing party could insist that the inspection take place in an area which is subject to surveillance, or could insist that only a certain limited number of documents be provided at one time, or could hire its own security guard, or could assign a member of its staff to supervise the inspection. These are all ordinary expenses connected with the cost of starting, or being involved in, a lawsuit. The court should carefully weigh the necessity of any additional burdens in the litigation process, given the existing high costs of that process. The court would not displace the general rule entitling a party to inspect documents for a general rule restricting a self-represented party's right to inspect produced documents by requiring that party to hire a lawyer for the purpose of attending at the inspection. A party who is represented by a lawyer should not be treated more harshly than a party who is self represented.
