The test for this non-disclosure order is that of a “real risk”… 3.
There is also a right to apply to the court to remove the document or other evidence in whole or in part from the implied undertaking or sealing order for use in other proceedings.

For example, to test the credibility of a witness where that witness has testified before in a proceeding in respect of the same subject matter and it can be shown that the evidence in this proceeding is or appears to be contrary thereto: see Alberta Evidence Act, R.S.A.
1(c) and 26.
Such application would also cover the possible situation where the discovery discloses fraudulent or criminal conduct.
However, notably, “The public interest in investigating possible crimes is not per se a sufficient ground to relieve counsel of his or her implied undertaking to keep such information private”… 4.
Counsel, as officers of the court, have a duty not to disclose or use oral evidence or documents outside the subject proceedings, so as to, at all times, honour the implied undertaking.
Counsel, as officers of the court who are not directly involved or involved at all in the proceeding have a similar obligation.
So as to not devalue the implied undertaking and in special circumstances, transcripts and copies of documents may be made available to parties outside the proceedings only with leave of the court.
Without leave, no use shall be made of the same by any person who by the discovery or trial process comes into such information or documents.
The implied undertaking and non-disclosure orders continue after the use of the information in court and thereafter except with leave of the court.
Wirth Ltd. v.
Acadia Pipe & Supply Corp.
L.R.
Madam Justice Coutu considered the matter in Ochitwa v.
Bombino (1997), 56 Alta.
L.R.
Her Ladyship agreed with Lutz J.'s comments in Wirth and further said, at pp.

42-44: It is clear that Alberta law imposes upon litigants an implied undertaking not to use information or documents for any purpose ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit in which they are discovered. . . . . .

If a party requesting the information to be produced later attempts to use the information for the purposes of another lawsuit, as against the parties who produced the information, the courts have held that that is in breach of the implied undertaking rule and have stayed the action as being an abuse of process… In the present case, the Plaintiff submits that the implied undertaking rule should cover only information that the receiving party could not otherwise have obtained by legitimate means independent of the litigation process and submits that the obligation is in favour of the producing party only, not third parties.
There is no necessity for narrowing the scope of the implied undertaking rule.

I agree with the broad rule that Lutz, J. set out, that is, the implied undertaking by the solicitors and the parties to an action is to maintain all information arising from the discovery process confidential in that it is not to be used for any collateral or ulterior purpose without leave of the court.
A party can apply to the court to remove the document or evidence in whole or in part from the implied undertaking.
The court has the discretion to review each particular case and make a determination whether it is in the public interest to remove the document or other evidence from the implied undertaking.

The fact that the information could have been obtained independent of the litigation process or that a third party is involved may be factors influencing a court to exercise its discretion to give relief from the undertaking.
There should not be a rigid rule that if either of these conditions existed the implied undertaking rule would not be applicable.
In the Carbone decision [Carbone v.
De La Rocha (1993), 13 O.R.
Gen.

Div.)] at page 367 the Court commented that the implied undertaking rule is still being developed: In summary, then, although the rule was initially expressed in terms of maintaining private proprietary interest and confidentiality, its ultimate foundation rests in the necessity to preserve the integrity of a process which:
(a) encourages and requires full disclosure in respect to the issues being litigated; and
(b) consequently promotes a just conclusion to the existing dispute, either by agreed settlement of the parties or the adjudication of the Court.
Whether and when the court will permit some collateral use of discovered information has not yet been fully or clearly explored.
Perhaps the variety of human affairs defies the development of comprehensive guidelines.

While the courts are sensitive to the intrusion occasioned to individual parties who are compelled to disclose, the sensitivity is secondary to the concern that such intrusion be strictly limited to the purpose of the litigation, less [sic] the system which depends upon full disclosure be undermined by purposes or motives outside the confines of the immediate process.
The individual interests are to be weighed against the public interests in an efficient and fair system of justice.
It is also clear that the courts do not wish to be perceived as instruments of purposes ulterior to the immediate issue they are being asked to resolve.
(emphasis Coutu J.'s) In Law Society (Alberta) v.
Randhawa (1996), 39 Alta.
L.R.

Justice LoVecchio considered the following issue arising from Wirth: does the implied undertaking of all lawyers to the court to use transcripts of examinations for discovery only for the purposes of the litigation in which they were taken, unless leave of the court is obtained, apply to lawyers acting for the Law Society who come into possession of those transcipts during the course of a bona fide Law Society investigation of one of its members?
At pp.

228-29, his Lordship said: Should Wirth be interpreted as an absolute rule with the incumbent corollary that relief from the rule may only be obtained by leave of the Court or should the rule be considered more limited and therefore not applicable in certain circumstances?

Without in any way stating whether there should be any other exceptions, for the reasons which follow, in my view the rule should not be construed as absolute in so far as it relates to the self regulatory matters contemplated by the Legal Profession Act.
At p.

231, he concluded: Having regard for the above, I do not believe I do any disservice to the logic or the wisdom of the Lutz, J. decision in Wirth by limiting the scope of the implied undertaking (so as not to require leave of the Court) when we are dealing with a Law Society investigation of one of its members for misconduct.
In a much different fact situation, the use of discovery transcripts was also addressed by the Court of Appeal.
In U.N.A. v.
Alberta Children's Hospital (1996), 40 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 128, a nurse was dismissed from her employment due to an inability to perform her duties as a result of a motor vehicle accident.
The nurse grieved her dismissal, and, in the grievance proceedings, the hospital requested transcripts from the accident litigation discoveries.
The issue was what, if any, implied undertakings attached to the produced transcripts.
At pp.

129-30, the court said: The grievor contended that she was bound by an implied undertaking not to disclose what was said on examination for discovery, and that the court should not relieve against that … The first issue is whether the implied undertaking binds or affects the grievor.
We know of no authority which says that the implied undertaking applies to her.

It is customarily expressed as an undertaking by a party to litigation who receives documents or information by the discovery process not to use what he or she receives for collateral purposes, without leave of the court.
Nor would the usual rationale expressed for the undertaking apply to a party who gives information on discovery as the grievor did.
Nor is this a case where the respondent hospital seeks to use a discovery transcript which it got from the former litigation opponents of the grievor, or indeed from any non-party.
The respondent hospital seeks the transcripts from the grievor herself.
However, we do not wish to foreclose discussion of that interesting topic in another case.

It is possible that other rationales do exist for creating some restriction on the use which non-parties may make of discovery transcripts, or for giving the witness on discovery some kind of privacy for some or all parts of the transcript of his or her answers on discovery.
There is much which might be said on both sides on such an issue.
There are many different factual situations which might arise, not all of them easy to forsee now.
What is relevant in one suit can be irrelevant in another, and indirectly relevant in a third.
What is disclosed in one suit may be harmless in another, and very harmful or embarrassing in a third.
In Casavant v.
Alberta Co-op Taxi Line Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 425 (Master), Master Funduk discussed the undertaking, to whom it is made, and the remedy for its breach.
At pp.

426-28 the learned Master said: Litigants are compelled by the court to discover and produce all documents which are or have been in their possession or power relating to all matters or questions in the lawsuit: Rules 186 and 189.
Litigants are compelled by the court to submit to an oral examination by any litigant adverse in interest: Rule 200.

Because of that compulsion the court says that documents obtained through the discovery process and information obtained from the oral examinations shall be used by the adverse litigants only for the purposes of the lawsuit.

The common statement is that what is obtained through the discovery process shall not be used for any purpose which is ulterior or collateral to the lawsuit … The court imposes an implied undertaking on the litigants that they will not use that information except for purposes related to the lawsuit.
It is done by the court as part of its inherent jurisidiction to control its own practice … Like coins, undertakings are not one sided.
The undertaking is by the litigant.
Who is it given to?
Alterskye v.
Scott, [1948] 1 All E.R.
D., says that a breach of the undertaking is contempt of court … That implies that the undertaking is given to the court, not the adverse litigant.
The learned Master then quoted from Alterskye and said: I do not read the last phrase to mean that the aggrieved litigant can sue for damages.
The aggrieved litigant can ask the court to expressly order the other litigant to stop the breach, if it is continuing.
That should be done by an application in the existing lawsuit because it relates to the conduct of the lawsuit… Harman[Home Office v.
Harman, [1983] A.C.
280 (H.L.)]… says that the implied undertaking is to the court.
Breach of that undertaking is a contempt of court.
Lord Diplock says that such a contempt of court would be civil, and the court would deal with it only on a motion by the other litigant.

Lord Keith of Kinkel says that the implied undertaking is owed not to the owner of the documents but to the court, and the function of the court in seeing that the obligation is observed is directed to the maintenance of the proper administration of justice and not to the enforcement of the law relating to confidentiality.
Lord Scarman says that the obligation is formulated as arising from an undertaking exacted by the court from the party and his solicitor to whom the documents are disclosed.
Breach of the obligation is a contempt of court… There is no cause of action for breach of the implied undertaking.
The remedy is to apply to have the employer held in contempt of court.
Also see the annotation: “Testimony in Other Proceedings” under R.
Also see the annotation “Implied Undertaking Regarding Confidentiality” under R.
Anton Piller Orders In Catalyst Partners Inc. v.
Meridian Packaging Ltd., 2007 ABCA 201, 2007 CarswellAlta 816, 417 A.R.
7, 76 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 264, the Court gave the following explanation of Anton Piller orders (at pp.
265-266): 5 The production of records is a normal step in all civil litigation.
Once pleadings are closed, each party is required to discover under oath all the relevant and material documents in its possession.
The rules on the discovery of records presume a considerable amount of good faith on the part of the litigants.

They presume that the litigants will not conceal or neglect to discover any relevant and material documents, and they also therefore assume that the litigants will not actually destroy any of those documents.
6 The Anton Piller order is an extraordinary remedy that displaces the normal rules on discovery of records.
Anton Piller orders are applied for ex-parte, usually before the defendant even knows that an action has been commenced.
The orders enable the plaintiff to attend at the premises of the defendant, without notice, and take possession of the records of the defendant.

They are highly intrusive orders, made without giving the defendant the opportunity to respond to the allegations, and are therefore subject to a number of procedural limitations designed to protect the defendant.
Anton Piller orders are extraordinary orders, and should not be routinely granted: Celanese Canada Inc. v.
Murray Demolition Corp., [2006] 2 S.C.R.
They are limited to extreme cases.
7 Celanese Canada at para.

35 sets out four essential conditions for the granting of an Anton Piller order: a) The plaintiff must demonstrate a strong prima facie case; b) The damage to the plaintiff of the defendant's alleged misconduct must be very serious; c) There must be convincing evidence that the defendant has in its possession incriminating documents or things; and d) It must be shown that there is a real possibility that the defendant may destroy such material before the discovery process can do its work.
Since the raison d'etre of an Anton Piller order is to preserve documents that might otherwise be destroyed, the fourth criterion is of central importance.
8 As mentioned, Anton Piller orders are always granted ex-parte.

The initial ex-parte order is frequently followed by a second review by the court, during which the defendant seeks to set aside the Anton Piller order, and the plaintiff seeks to have the order confirmed and the seized documents released to it.

By the time of the second stage the defendant will have had an opportunity to file evidence, the plaintiff may well have supplemented its evidence, and there will likely have been cross-examination on the various affidavits.
It follows that the evidence at the second de novo stage of the process might well be different than that available on the original ex-parte application.
Electronic Records In Questor Technology Inc v.
Stagg, 2022 ABQB 578, 2022 CarswellAlta 2372, Justice D.

Nixon discussed production of records which exist in multiple formats: [114] Where records exist in multiple formats, including their native format, they must be produced: Bard v Canadian Natural Resources, 2016 ABQB 267 at para 96 [Bard], citing 2038724 Ontario Ltd v Quizno's Canada Restaurant Corp, 2012 ONSC 6549 at paras 128–131[Quizno's].

The production of documents in non-native format is not as meaningful and does not permit the plaintiff to take full advantage of available technology as documents available in their native format: Gamble v MGI Securities, 2011 ONSC 2705 at para 22.
[115] In Bard, the Court considered whether it should order a party to produce records in a format importable into Microsoft Excel: Bard at paras 96–115.
The party resisting disclosure argued that it did not keep records in this file format and that it would be significantly costly for it to produce the files: Bard paras 101–104.
Notwithstanding the arguments of the resisting party in Bard, the Court in that case ordered the native files to be created and produced: Bard at para 125.
In doing so, the Court noted the importance of usable files in resolving disputes: Usability is as much a concern for a litigant as it is for the Court.
Producing records in an unusable format undermines procedural fairness and just results.

It does not help to narrow the issues in dispute, and not only impairs the plaintiff's ability to prove its case, but also threatens the Court's ability to understand the evidence put before it …: Bard at para 115. … [121] Metadata is a producible record where relevant and material: Spar at para 75-76.
Where the timing of the treatment of records, including when they were modified, and the dates and tracking routes of emails are at issue in litigation, metadata will be producible: Spar at para 76.
In Spar Aerospace Ltd. v.
Aerowerks Engineering Inc., 2007 ABQB 543, 2007 CarswellAlta 1156, 428 A.R.
84, 80 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 123; affirmed 2008 ABCA 47, 2008 CarswellAlta 143, 85 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 14, Veit J. made the following general comment in respect of the production of electronic records (at p.
L.R.

(4th) 123]): … the production of electronic records should be produced electronically; hence, the party to whom the records are produced is entitled to all passwords, operating systems and system-related files to allow real access to the produced material.
Her Ladyship then made these specific comments (at pp.
141-142): 68 The defendants are required to provide to Spar all passwords, systems and software necessary to access the records produced.
69 Here, the defendants have provided approximately 1.2 gigabytes of information, much of which is password protected and therefore inaccessible to Spar.

70 It was always the case that production included an obligation to provide all technical information necessary to allow the receiving party to access the production: Canadian Engineering and Surveys (Yukon) Limited.
71 That general principle carries over to electronic disclosure.

Moreover, it is obvious that the defendants should produce their electronic records electronically: not only is hard copy production considerably more expensive, but it is also less searchable and is inferior because it does not retain potentially critical meta- data such as when and by whom a record was created or amended: Cholakis.

In order to access the electronic disclosure, it is obvious that a receiving party requires from the producing party whatever passwords and other systems necessary in order to constitute real disclosure. d) Must unprocessed records be produced?
72 The defendants must produce their electronic records in a meaningful way.
Here the electronic records provided have not been processed for export into an electronic document database program.
73 The principles of meaningful disclosure are the same, whether disclosure is made by electronic or paper means: Wilson, Prism Hospital Software Inc., Nicolardi. e) Must metadata be produced?
74 In the circumstances here, the defendants must produce their metadata.
75 Metada is a record: Desgagne.

76 While metada presumably need not be produced in most situations, because it is irrelevant to know, for example, when a document was printed, the production of such records is material and relevant here where the pleadings disclose that the identity of the author of electronic records, the timing of the treatment of those records—including if and when they were modified, the dates and tracking routes of e-mail, are all potentially at the very core of the issues that are raised in the litigation.
Must the hard drives be produced?
77 Spar has proven its entitlement to access to the defendants' hard drives and is entitled to immediate access to them.
78 It goes without saying, that access to the opponent's hard drives will not always be granted by a court: Baldwin Janzen, Ireland.… 4.

Translation of Documents What is before me is whether a litigant has complied if he undertakes to produce documents and he has in fact produced them but they are in a different language than the opposite party expected.
They may well be in a different language than the producing party expected as well, and it is almost implicit from the context of this application that that is what happened here.
It may well be that Mr.
Erler would not have undertaken to produce those documents if he knew they were in the German language and was required to translate them.
In my view the proper approach is to ask who wants the documents and for whose benefit are they produced.
The plaintiff has not suggested it needs the documents or that it will be relying on them.

The defendants are the ones who want the documents and obviously they have no idea whether they will be relying on them until they know the content of those documents … If the defendants want to see what these documents are all about they will have to accept the time and cost risks inherent in translating them.
In my view the plaintiff has complied with the undertakings.
Jasper Millwork Ltd. v.
Borden Co.
L.R.
(3d) 181 (Master), at 183, per Master Breitkreuz.
The Imposition of Conditions Will Be Unusual In B.E.
Kennedy Design Ltd. v.
Kibo Group Inc., 2000 ABQB 429, 2000 CarswellAlta 659, 269 A.R.
156; additional reasons at 2001 ABQB 32, 2001 CarswellAlta 2630, 304 A.R.
2, an individual defendant wanted to inspect the plaintiff's records pursuant to Rule 193.
The plaintiff wanted the court to impose a condition that the defendant's lawyer accompany the defendant during the inspection.
The Court refused to do so.
Veit, J. said, at pp.
157-158: A party has a right to inspect the documents produced for discovery by parties opposite; that right should only be restricted where circumstances warrant.
At this pre-trial stage, each party has an obligation to protect their own documents, and indeed has a self-interest in doing so.
The documents that are produced on discovery are not necessarily going to be exhibits at trial; therefore, the court does not yet have an obligation to safeguard these documents.
The exercise of the right to inspection should not be limited by imposing a financial burden on the inspecting party.
The Rule points the way to the right result in this matter: if a party wants a copy of a document, that copy will be made at the inspecting party's expense.
However, the mere inspection of the documents is a right, not something which the inspecting party must pay for.
The producing party can impose a framework on the inspection which will promote the security of the documents.

For example, the producing party could insist that the inspection take place in an area which is subject to surveillance, or could insist that only a certain limited number of documents be provided at one time, or could hire its own security guard, or could assign a member of its staff to supervise the inspection.
These are all ordinary expenses connected with the cost of starting, or being involved in, a lawsuit.
The court should carefully weigh the necessity of any additional burdens in the litigation process, given the existing high costs of that process.

The court would not displace the general rule entitling a party to inspect documents for a general rule restricting a self-represented party's right to inspect produced documents by requiring that party to hire a lawyer for the purpose of attending at the inspection.
A party who is represented by a lawyer should not be treated more harshly than a party who is self represented.

sentences.text: Admissions of authenticity of records

paragraphs.text: (1) In this rule, “authentic” includes the fact that (a) a document that is said to be an original was printed, written, signed or executed as it purports to have been, and (b) a document that is said to be a copy is a true copy of the original. (2) Subject to subrules (3), (4), (5) and (6), a party who makes an affidavit of records or on whose behalf an affidavit of records is filed and a party on whom an affidavit of records is served are both presumed to admit that (a) a record specified or referred to in the affidavit is authentic, and (b) if a record purports or appears to have been transmitted, the original was sent by the sender and was received by the addressee. (3) Subrule (2) (a) does not apply if the maker or the recipient of the affidavit objects in accordance with subrule (4), (b) does not prejudice the right of a party to object to the admission of a record in evidence, and (c) does not constitute an agreement or acknowledgment that the record is relevant and material. (4) The maker or recipient of an affidavit of records is not presumed to make the admission referred to in subrule (2) if, within 3 months after the date on which the records are produced, the maker or recipient serves notice on the other party that the authenticity or transmittal of a record, as the case may be, is disputed and that it must be proved at trial. (5) Notwithstanding that the maker or recipient of an affidavit of records does not serve a notice under subrule (4) within the time provided by that subrule, the Court may order that the maker or recipient is not presumed to make the admission referred to in subrule (2). (6) This rule does not apply to a record whose authenticity, receipt or transmission has been denied by a party in the party's pleadings. Alta. Reg. 140/2013, s. 6

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.15:1 Rule 5.15 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.15. Practice Note One must remember the obligations imposed by R. 5.15 when the affidavit of records is received. A failure to review the affidavit and, within three months after the records are produced, contest one or more of the matters set forth in R. 5.15(2) will result in deemed admissions: First National Bank of Oregon v. A.H. Watson Ranching Ltd. (1984), 34 Alta. L.R. (2d) 110 at 131-32 (Q.B.), is an example of this. In Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, 2002 ABCA 110, 2002 CarswellAlta 603, 303 A.R. 43, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1; additional reasons at 2002 ABCA 150, 2002 CarswellAlta 788, 303 A.R. 43 at 61, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 24, the court said, at p. 6: In general, an affidavit of records does not transform any of the records (documents) listed in any of its schedules into evidence. There are only two narrow exceptions, both created by R. 192(1). It deems that both parties (sides) admit that (a) those records “are authentic”, and (b) if copies of letters or messages appear to have been sent, the originals were sent and were received by the addressee. We consider ‘authentic’ to mean that the record is what it purports to be and is not a forgery. It probably also means that if it purports to be a copy, it is an accurate copy. An affidavit of records never makes a record evidence of the truth of its contents. For example, most affidavits of records would list or identify a demand letter by the plaintiff to the defendant. That would be prima facie evidence that demand was made, but it would be no evidence whatever that the demand was well founded, or that any facts alleged in the demand letter were true. Furthermore, there are exceptions to deemed admissions (a) and (b) above. A notice of non-admission may be given (or included in the affidavit of records: R. 192(3)). The party who is deemed to admit authenticity, despatch, and receipt of a message may still object to its admissibility in evidence (R. 192(2)(b)). And the entire rule on these deemed admissions ceases to apply at all, if the pleadings of the party deny the authenticity or receipt or despatch of a record (document) (R. 192(6)). Of course a letter might contain an admission by the author, and so be admissible at common law against him, once there was proof (or deemed proof) of authenticity of the letter. 1. Production does not acknowledge admissibility of a record What is Relevancy? While I do agree that Rule 198 of our Rules of Court states that the disclosure of the existence of a document in an affidavit of documents does not prevent the discloser from later arguing the relevancy or admissibility of the document, nevertheless, the fact that it was disclosed in the first instance indicates that the matter of relevancy or admissibility was at least present in the mind of the discloser and it is up to the court to decide upon its ultimate use in the action. Leeds v. Alberta (Minister of the Environment) (1990), 69 D.L.R. (4th) 681 (Alta. Q.B.), at 685-86, per Miller A.C.J.Q.B. Master Funduk stated: This document does not deal with private approach roads so it is irrelevant. It does not become relevant just because the County produced it. Relevance is determined by the issues in the lawsuit, not by whether a document is produced. The discovery of a document is not an admission of its relevance (rule 198) so I do not see why its production is deemed to be an admission that it is relevant. If a party discovers a document he must produce it (subject to claims for privilege). It would be illogical to say that its discovery is not an admission of relevance but its production (which is required) is an admission of relevance. Rohr v. Hosack (1991), 119 A.R. 177 at 183 (Master). In County of Vulcan v. Genesis Reciprocal Insurance Exchange, 2020 ABQB 93, 2020 CarswellAlta 192, Justice Graesser said: [84] The Rule does not make documents in an affidavit of records presumptively admissible in evidence, nor does it make the contents of the documents evidence of the truth of the document's contents (see Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at paragraph 6 and following). 2. Admission is binding on both parties In First Calgary Holdings (Alb) Corp. v. Metropolitan Ventures Inc., 2015 ABQB 54, 2015 CarswellAlta 108 (Master), Master Robertson said, at paragraph 40: 40 It is important to note that when an affidavit of records is served, unless there is a denial of authenticity (set out in Rule 5.15(4)), the deemed authenticity and transmission is binding on both parties—not just on the party who served the affidavit of records.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.16:1 Rule 5.16 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.16. 1. Overview In ATCO Energy Solutions Ltd. V. Energy Dynamics Ltd., 2024 ABKB 162, Justice Marion said: [47] Relief under rule 5.16 is not intended to be the norm. Rule 5.16 and rule 5.10 are designed to avoid trial by ambush and its associated unfairness: Smith v Smith, 2016 ABCA 376 at para 42; Signalta Resources Limited v Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2022 ABQB 89 at paras 34-35 [Signalta]. They are also to avoid last-minute trial adjournments and the waste of public and judicial resources. [48] Whether to allow a party to use a record when they have not complied with rule 5.16 is in the court’s discretion. However, in order exercise its discretion the court must do so “on the basis that there was a sufficient reason for the failure to disclose”: rule 5.16. In this respect, I agree with Terrigno v Fox, 2023 ABKB 89 at paras 77-82 [Terrigno]: the explanation for the non-disclosure is the first line of inquiry. A strong interpretation of rule 5.16 is necessary to fulfil its purpose of avoiding trial unfairness and wasteful delays. [49] Even if the court is satisfied that a non-disclosing party had a sufficient reason for its late or failed disclosure, then the court may consider other factors before exercising its discretion, including whether the other party would suffer prejudice if the use of the record is permitted, whether excluding the record would prevent the determination of the issue on the merits, and whether, in the circumstances of the case, the ends of justice require that the record be admitted: Terrigno at para 78; Signalta at paras 42-49 citing Stone v Ellerman, 2009 BCCA 294. This is not an exhaustive list of considerations.

sentences.text: People who may be questioned

paragraphs.text: (1) A party is entitled to ask the following persons questions under oath about relevant and material records and relevant and material information: (a) each of the other parties who is adverse in interest; (b) if the party adverse in interest is a corporation, (i) one or more officers or former officers of the corporation who have or appear to have relevant and material information that was acquired because they are or were officers of the corporation, and (ii) the corporate representative; (c) if a litigation representative is appointed for a party, (i) the litigation representative, and (ii) with the Court's permission, the person on whose behalf the litigation representative is appointed if that person is competent to give evidence; (d) one or more other persons who are or were employees of the party adverse in interest who have or appear to have relevant and material information that was acquired because of the employment; (e) an auditor or former auditor engaged by a party adverse in interest, but not an auditor or former auditor engaged solely for the purpose of the action; (f) if a partnership is a party adverse in interest, a partner or former partner of the partnership; (g) in an action with respect to a negotiable instrument or chose in action, (i) an assignor of the negotiable instrument or chose in action, (ii) a prior endorser, drawer, holder or maker of the negotiable instrument, and (iii) an employee or former employee of an assignor of the negotiable instrument or chose in action, and if the assignor is a corporation, an officer or former officer of the corporation. (2) If a questioning party questions more than one person of a party adverse in interest under subrule (1) and the person questioned is (a) an officer or former officer of a corporation described in subrule (1)(b)(i), (b) an employee or former employee of the party adverse in interest described in subrule (1)(d), (c) an auditor or former auditor described in subrule (1)(e), (d) a partner or former partner of a partnership referred to in subrule (1)(f), or (e) an employee, former employee, officer or former officer described in subrule (1)(g)(iii), other than a corporate representative, the costs of questioning the second and subsequent persons are to be paid by the questioning party unless (f) the parties otherwise agree, or (g) the Court otherwise orders. (3) This rule applies whether the person to be questioned is within or outside the Court's jurisdiction.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.17:1 Rule 5.17 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.17. 1. “True Parties” Approach to Questioning In Golden Estate v. Neilson, 2011 ABCA 338, 2011 CarswellAlta 2281, the defendants sought an order compelling the deceased's mother and spouse to attend for questioning under R. 5.17. The deceased (Tyson Golden) “committed suicide within days of his release from the hospital.” The Public Trustee, as the personal representative of the estate of the deceased, brought an action against the attending physicians and Capital Health (operator of the hospital). The action was brought on behalf of the estate (for funeral expenses), the parents (for statutory bereavement), and the deceased's spouse and child (for statutory bereavement and loss of financial support). The Court of Appeal, at paragraph 7 set out the reason for the defendants' application: “From the documents and information obtained at discovery, the [defendants] question whether the deceased's mother and spouse may have failed to take reasonable steps to monitor and assist the deceased upon his discharge from hospital, giving rise to a possible break in the chain of causation. The [defendants] seek further information from the deceased's mother and spouse in this regard.” The learned Chambers judge denied the defendants' application to question the deceased's mother and spouse, ruling that they were not parties adverse in interest to the defendnats. The Court of Appeal allowed the defendants' appeal. At paragraphs 14–19, and 21, the Court said: 14 Rule 5.17(1)(a) of the new Rules of Court states that a party is entitled to ask “other parties who [are] adverse in interest” questions under oath about relevant and material records and relevant and material information. 15 The deceased's mother and spouse were not named as parties in the style of cause; but the prayer for relief claims relief on their behalf (as well as on behalf of the estate). And the statement of claim seeks that relief against the appellants on the basis that they negligently caused the deceased's death. 16 A person for whose benefit an action is prosecuted is regarded as a party to the lawsuit: Re Cantalini and Hirtz. 17 The chambers judge properly concluded that the deceased's mother and spouse were “parties” on the authorities just cited. However, she also concluded that the deceased's mother and spouse were not “adverse in interest” to the appellants because they did not have a cause of action against the appellants. In the chambers judge's view, the only entity with a cause of action against the appellants was the deceased's estate and then only by virtue of the Fatal Accidents Act, RSA 2000, c F-8. 18 However, section 3(1) of the Fatal Accidents Act expressly confers a cause of action on the spouse, parents and children of a deceased. The action must be brought in the name of an executor or administrator if there is one. If not, or if the executor or administrator does not bring the action within one year, the action may be brought in the name of any or all of the persons for whose benefit the action would have been brought if it had been brought by the executor or administrator, in this case, the parents, the spouse and the child of the deceased. But the cause of action is that of the parents, the spouse or the child of the person whose death is alleged to have been caused by the wrongful act, neglect or default of another. Subsections 3(1) and 3(2) of the Fatal Accidents Act make it clear that the action may be brought either by an executor or administrator or, failing that, by the parties themselves […] 19 In our view, the chambers judge erred in concluding that the mother and spouse of the deceased were not adverse in interest to the appellants. They are the persons for whose benefit the claim for relief was brought, and could have brought the claim on their own behalf had the Public Trustee failed to do so. They also have personal knowledge of facts essential to establish the claim and will undoubtedly be witnesses at any trial. We conclude that parties on whose behalf a claim is brought under the Fatal Accidents Act, or who claim relief directly under the Fatal Accidents Act are parties adverse in interest to the party or parties whose negligence or wrongful acts are alleged to have caused the death of the deceased. … 21 In conclusion, we have adopted a “true parties” approach to the assessment of questioning under the new Rules. In our opinion, the mother and the spouse of the deceased are, indeed, true parties whose evidence would enhance speed, economy, fairness and disclosure, the factors referred to in Wilbur v Miller, 2005 ABCA 220 at para. 11, 367 AR 191. Not only are the claimants in a position to provide essential evidence, they are also in a position to provide the best evidence on the issues of entitlement, liability and quantum, issues which flow from the Fatal Accidents Act and the Survival of Actions Act, RSA 2000, c S-27. In KJM v. Kuc, 2024 ABCA 388, the Court gave further guidance on the issue of whom may be questioned. In particular, the Court explained that its decision in Golden Estate v. Neilson, supra, should not be read too broadly. In KJM v. Kuc, supra, the infant plaintiff suffered at birth injuries alleged to have been caused by alleged breaches of duty by the defendants. The defendants applied for an order allowing them to question the infant's mother. The mother was not the litigation representative of the infant plaintiff, nor otherwise a party to the action. The learned chambers justice dismissed the application and the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The Court of Appeal said: [5] The Rules of Court set out in detail who can be questioned before trial. The rules applicable to the present application are as follows:
